claim: Roman history is usually divided into the Kingdom, the Republic (from 509 BCE) and the Empire (from 27 BCE).
tested_by: L1 question.ancient_rome.001.q1; L2 question.ancient_rome.002.q3; L3 question.ancient_rome.003.q3; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q1; L99 question.ancient_rome.099.q3
pre_check: Conventional dates; confirm the page uses them.
fact_check_evidence: Standard references divide ancient Rome into the Kingdom (753 to 509 BCE), Republic (509 to 27 BCE) and Empire (from 27 BCE). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/the-roman-republic-509-bce-to-27-bce.html)

claim: The last emperor in the West, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed in 476 CE, the usual date given for the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
appears_in: L1 card.ancient_rome.001.c4; L93 card.ancient_rome.093.c3; L99 card.ancient_rome.099.c2
fact_check_evidence: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus on 4 September 476; this is the date most commonly given for the end of the Western Roman Empire, though not the only one. (https://www.history.com/articles/last-roman-emperor-romulus-augustulus https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire)

claim: The eastern half of the empire, ruled from Constantinople, lasted until the city fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453.
appears_in: L1 card.ancient_rome.001.c4; L95 card.ancient_rome.095.c1; L95 card.ancient_rome.095.c4; L99 card.ancient_rome.099.c2
fact_check_evidence: Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks under Mehmed II on 29 May 1453, ending the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire. (https://www.britannica.com/event/Fall-of-Constantinople-1453 https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-worldhistory/chapter/the-fall-of-constantinople/)

claim: Roman tradition dated the founding of Rome to 753 BCE.
appears_in: L1 card.ancient_rome.001.c2; L10 card.ancient_rome.010.c2; L21 card.ancient_rome.021.c4; L99 card.ancient_rome.099.c2
tested_by: L1 question.ancient_rome.001.q1; L2 question.ancient_rome.002.q3; L3 question.ancient_rome.003.q3; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q1; L99 question.ancient_rome.099.q3
fact_check_evidence: Varro settled on 753 BC, which became the accepted traditional date (21 April 753 BC) for Rome's founding. (https://www.historytoday.com/archive/months-past/foundation-rome https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varronian_chronology)

claim: At its height the Roman Empire surrounded the Mediterranean, stretching from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to the Middle East.
fact_check_evidence: Under Trajan the empire held nearly all Mediterranean shores, from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to Mesopotamia. (https://www.worldatlas.com/ancient-world/how-big-was-the-roman-empire-at-its-peak.html https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/roman-empire-size/)

claim: Romans called the Mediterranean Mare Nostrum, “our sea.”
fact_check_evidence: Mare Nostrum ('our sea') was the Roman name for the Mediterranean. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mare_Nostrum https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/curiosities/mare-nostrum-our-sea/amp/)

claim: According to legend, Rome was founded by the twins Romulus and Remus, sons of the god Mars, who were abandoned as babies and nursed by a she-wolf.
tested_by: L2 question.ancient_rome.002.q1; L47 question.ancient_rome.047.q3; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q1
fact_check_evidence: In the legend the twins, sons of Rhea Silvia and Mars, were abandoned by the Tiber, suckled by a she-wolf, and later set out to found the city (Romulus prevailing). (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/myth-romulus-and-remus https://www.rome.net/romulus-and-remus)

claim: The she-wolf nursing the twins became one of Rome’s best-known symbols.
tested_by: L2 question.ancient_rome.002.q1; L47 question.ancient_rome.047.q3; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q1
fact_check_evidence: The she-wolf nursing Romulus and Remus was a symbol of Rome from antiquity and remains one of its best-known emblems. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitoline_Wolf https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/ancient-art-civilizations/roman/roman-republic/a/capitoline-she-wolf)

claim: In the legend, Romulus killed Remus in a quarrel over the new city, which was named after Romulus.
fact_check_evidence: In the common version of the legend the twins quarreled over the city's site and Romulus killed Remus; the city was named Roma after Romulus. Some versions differ in detail. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus http://www.thelatinlibrary.com/legacy/livy/romulus.html)

claim: Romans also traced their ancestry to Aeneas, a Trojan prince who, in legend, fled the fall of Troy to Italy.
tested_by: L2 question.ancient_rome.002.q2; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q4; L47 question.ancient_rome.047.q3
fact_check_evidence: World History Encyclopedia and the Aeneid entry: Aeneas, a Trojan prince, escaped the fall of Troy and in legend reached Italy, becoming the ancestor of the Romans. (https://www.worldhistory.org/Aeneas/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)

claim: Historians treat Rome’s founding stories as legend: they were written down centuries after the events they describe.
tested_by: L2 question.ancient_rome.002.q2; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q4; L47 question.ancient_rome.047.q3
fact_check_evidence: The earliest written accounts of Rome's founding (e.g. Fabius Pictor, c. 200 BCE) date some five centuries after the traditional 753 BCE date; historians treat them as legend. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_and_Remus)

claim: The first Romans were Latins, a people of the region of Latium in central Italy.
tested_by: L3 question.ancient_rome.003.q1; L3 question.ancient_rome.003.q3; L4 question.ancient_rome.004.q3; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q3
fact_check_evidence: The Latins, an Italic people of Latium in west-central Italy, included the early inhabitants of Rome. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latins_(Italic_tribe) https://www.britannica.com/place/Latium)

claim: Archaeologists have found traces of Iron Age huts on the Palatine Hill from around the 8th century BCE, close to the traditional founding date.
appears_in: L3 card.ancient_rome.003.c1; L3 card.ancient_rome.003.c2; L10 card.ancient_rome.010.c2
tested_by: L3 question.ancient_rome.003.q1; L3 question.ancient_rome.003.q3; L4 question.ancient_rome.004.q3; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q3
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions the hut remains and their dating.
fact_check_evidence: Postholes of Iron Age huts on the Palatine (including the so-called Casa Romuli area) are dated to Latial phase III, the late 9th to 8th century BCE. (https://www.digitalaugustanrome.org/records/casa-romuli-palatium/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_Romuli)

claim: Early Rome grew from small hilltop villages that gradually merged into one community.
tested_by: L3 question.ancient_rome.003.q2; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q3; L61 question.ancient_rome.061.q3
fact_check_evidence: Archaeology indicates Rome formed by gradual union (synoecism) of hilltop villages such as those on the Palatine and Quirinal. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_of_Rome https://www.sociostudies.org/journal/files/seh/2010_2/the_archaeology_of_early_state_in_italy.pdf)

claim: The valley that became the Roman Forum was once marshy and was drained, helped by the great drain later called the Cloaca Maxima.
appears_in: L3 card.ancient_rome.003.c3; L3 card.ancient_rome.003.c4; L10 card.ancient_rome.010.c2
tested_by: L3 question.ancient_rome.003.q2; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q3; L61 question.ancient_rome.061.q3
fact_check_evidence: The Forum site was a marshy area drained under the Tarquins by works that became the Cloaca Maxima; the Forum was laid out in the drained valley. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloaca_Maxima https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Forum)

claim: The valley that became the Roman Forum was once marshy and was drained, helped by the great drain later called the Cloaca Maxima.
appears_in: L3 card.ancient_rome.003.c3; L3 card.ancient_rome.003.c4; L10 card.ancient_rome.010.c2
tested_by: L3 question.ancient_rome.003.q2; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q3; L61 question.ancient_rome.061.q3
fact_check_evidence: The Forum site was a marshy area drained under the Tarquins by works that became the Cloaca Maxima; the Forum was laid out in the drained valley. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloaca_Maxima https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Forum)

claim: Parts of the Cloaca Maxima still carry water today.
pre_check: Confirm current use is stated.
fact_check_evidence: Sources state the Cloaca Maxima is still in use, draining rainwater from the Forum area, with surviving sections linked into Rome's modern drainage system. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloaca_Maxima https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/cloaca-maxima)

claim: Rome grew where the Tiber River could be crossed, near an island in the river, about 25 km from the sea.
tested_by: L4 question.ancient_rome.004.q1; L5 question.ancient_rome.005.q3; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q5
pre_check: Distance to the coast is approximate; confirm.
fact_check_evidence: Rome lies on the Tiber about 25 km (16 mi) from the sea at Ostia; the Tiber Island area was the site of an important ancient ford (a JRS study notes the island itself formed around the late 6th century BCE). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiber https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-roman-studies/article/origins-of-the-tiber-island-in-rome/E60CC18343D11A40BE8E436E2AF07FC4)

claim: An ancient salt route, later called the Via Salaria, passed through Rome’s site, linking the coast with inland Italy.
tested_by: L4 question.ancient_rome.004.q1; L5 question.ancient_rome.005.q3; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q5
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions the salt route.
fact_check_evidence: The Via Salaria is named for salt: it was the ancient route by which Sabines from inland fetched salt from the marshes at the Tiber mouth, passing the site of Rome. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Salaria)

claim: Ancient Rome was built on seven hills beside the Tiber, among them the Palatine and the Capitoline.
fact_check_evidence: Rome's seven hills lie east of the Tiber and include the Palatine and Capitoline. (https://www.britannica.com/place/Seven-Hills-of-Rome https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/what-are-the-seven-hills-of-rome.html)

claim: The hills were easier to defend and stayed dry when the Tiber flooded the low ground between them.
fact_check_evidence: Early villages occupied the hills, which rose from low marshy ground, retreating to hilltops for defense; the hills were safe from flooding of the low areas. (https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Ancient_History/Rome/Early_Rome_(the_Seven_Hills) http://engineeringrome.org/the-past-present-and-future-of-flood-control-in-rome/)

claim: Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, became Rome’s port, through which grain and other goods reached the city.
fact_check_evidence: Ostia, at the Tiber's mouth, served as Rome's port for grain and other goods (later supplemented by Portus). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostia_Antica https://www.unrv.com/articles/ostia-and-the-grain-supply-of-ancient-rome.php)

claim: The Etruscans lived in Etruria, the region north of Rome covering most of what is now Tuscany, plus parts of Lazio and Umbria.
fact_check_evidence: Etruria lay between the Arno and Tiber rivers, covering most of modern Tuscany plus northern Lazio and north-western Umbria, not Tuscany alone. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etruria https://www.britannica.com/place/Etruria-ancient-country-Italy)

claim: The Etruscans were organized in independent cities and were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy.
fact_check_evidence: Etruscans had no central government; independent city-states (a league of Twelve Peoples) dominated much of Italy at their 6th-century BCE peak. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Etruscan https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etruscan_civilization)

claim: The Etruscan language is unrelated to Latin and is still only partly understood.
fact_check_evidence: Etruscan was non-Indo-European and unrelated to Latin; grammar and many words are known but it is not fully understood. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Etruscan-language https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etruscan_language)

claim: According to Roman tradition, the last three kings of Rome were Etruscans.
fact_check_evidence: Tradition lists seven kings, the last three (Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius, Tarquinius Superbus) forming an Etruscan dynasty. (https://www.thecollector.com/etruscan-kings-of-rome/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Tarquinius_Priscus)

claim: According to Roman tradition, the last three kings of Rome were Etruscans.
fact_check_evidence: Tradition lists seven kings, the last three (Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius, Tarquinius Superbus) forming an Etruscan dynasty. (https://www.thecollector.com/etruscan-kings-of-rome/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Tarquinius_Priscus)

claim: The fasces, a bundle of rods around an axe carried before Roman officials as a sign of authority, came from the Etruscans.
tested_by: L5 question.ancient_rome.005.q2; L7 question.ancient_rome.007.q3; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q2
fact_check_evidence: Romans held the fasces came from the Etruscans, and a 7th-century BCE miniature iron fasces from an Etruscan tomb at Vetulonia supports this. Lictors carried them before magistrates as a symbol of imperium. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/fasces https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fasces)

claim: Romans learned haruspicy, reading omens in the organs of sacrificed animals, from the Etruscans.
tested_by: L5 question.ancient_rome.005.q2; L7 question.ancient_rome.007.q3; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q2
fact_check_evidence: Haruspicy was an Etruscan discipline that Rome adopted, employing Etruscan haruspices (the practice ultimately had Near Eastern roots). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haruspex https://www.britannica.com/topic/haruspicy)

claim: Roman tradition counted seven kings, from Romulus to Tarquin the Proud, ruling from 753 to 509 BCE.
appears_in: L6 card.ancient_rome.006.c2; L10 card.ancient_rome.010.c2; L10 card.ancient_rome.010.c3
fact_check_evidence: Roman tradition held that seven kings, Romulus to Tarquinius Superbus, ruled from 753 to 509 BCE; the claim is framed as tradition. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Rome https://courses.lumenlearning.com/atd-herkimer-westerncivilization/chapter/the-seven-kings/)

claim: Roman kingship was not simply inherited: tradition says most kings were chosen with the approval of the Senate and the people.
pre_check: Confirm the page describes the choice of kings.
fact_check_evidence: Tradition says kings after Romulus were nominated by an interrex, confirmed by the Senate and voted by the curiate assembly, but Romulus founded the city and Tarquin the Proud seized power without election, so 'each king' overstates it. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Rome https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Kingdom)

claim: Numa Pompilius, the second king, was remembered as the founder of Rome’s religious institutions and calendar.
fact_check_evidence: Tradition credits Numa, the second king, with the religious calendar and early religious institutions such as the Vestals, flamines and pontifex maximus. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Numa-Pompilius https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numa_Pompilius)

claim: Servius Tullius, the sixth king, was credited with the first census, which organized citizens by wealth.
fact_check_evidence: Tradition credits Servius Tullius, sixth king, with the census and the Servian constitution dividing citizens into classes by wealth; the claim is framed as tradition. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servius_Tullius https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servian_constitution)

claim: The Roman Senate began as a council of elders advising the king.
fact_check_evidence: Senate derives from senex (old man); under the kings it was an advisory council of elders (patres) acting as the king's council. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Senate https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/senate/)

claim: Before major public decisions Romans consulted augurs, priests who read the will of the gods in the flight of birds; unfavorable signs could delay public business.
fact_check_evidence: Augurs interpreted auspices, chiefly bird flight, to judge divine approval of public acts; unfavourable signs could postpone assemblies and elections (obnuntiatio). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augury https://ancientromelive.org/augury-and-the-will-of-the-gods/)

claim: The Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta, goddess of the hearth, which was never allowed to go out.
tested_by: L7 question.ancient_rome.007.q1; L88 question.ancient_rome.088.q3; L96 question.ancient_rome.096.q3
fact_check_evidence: The Vestals tended the eternal flame of Vesta, goddess of the hearth, which could never be allowed to go out; letting it die was punished. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_fire_of_Vesta https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestal_Virgin)

claim: Roman households honored the Lares and Penates, guardian spirits of the home and its food store, at a household shrine.
tested_by: L7 question.ancient_rome.007.q2; L8 question.ancient_rome.008.q3; L46 question.ancient_rome.046.q3; L84 question.ancient_rome.084.q2
fact_check_evidence: Lares and Penates were protective spirits of the household and its food supply (Penates tied to the penus, the storeroom), honored at the lararium shrine. (https://www.unrv.com/culture/lararium-lares-penates.php https://www.britannica.com/topic/Lar-Roman-deities)

claim: Roman religion stressed performing rituals correctly; the aim was to keep the pax deorum, peace with the gods.
tested_by: L7 question.ancient_rome.007.q2; L8 question.ancient_rome.008.q3; L46 question.ancient_rome.046.q3; L84 question.ancient_rome.084.q2
fact_check_evidence: Roman religion was orthopraxic, focused on correct ritual performance to maintain the pax deorum (peace with the gods). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Deorum https://www.unrv.com/culture/pax-deorum.php)

claim: Rome’s greatest temple, on the Capitoline Hill, was dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods, together with Juno and Minerva.
tested_by: L7 question.ancient_rome.007.q1; L88 question.ancient_rome.088.q3; L96 question.ancient_rome.096.q3
fact_check_evidence: The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline was Rome's most important temple, dedicated to the Capitoline Triad: Jupiter, Juno and Minerva. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Jupiter_Optimus_Maximus https://www.museicapitolini.org/en/infopage/temple-de-jupiter-capitolin)

claim: The paterfamilias, the oldest living male of a family, held legal power over his children and grandchildren, even as adults.
tested_by: L8 question.ancient_rome.008.q1; L8 question.ancient_rome.008.q2; L69 question.ancient_rome.069.q3
fact_check_evidence: The pater familias, the oldest living male ascendant, held patria potestas over his children, including adults, and grandchildren through sons until his death. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pater_familias https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100310590)

claim: In early Roman law this power, patria potestas, in theory included the power of life and death over family members.
tested_by: L8 question.ancient_rome.008.q1; L8 question.ancient_rome.008.q2; L69 question.ancient_rome.069.q3
fact_check_evidence: Early Roman law gave the paterfamilias the ius vitae necisque (power of life and death) over those in his potestas; it was rarely used and faded, being abolished in the 4th century CE. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pater_familias https://www.unrv.com/culture/patria-potestas.php)

claim: A Roman familia meant the whole household, including the enslaved people who lived and worked in it.
pre_check: Confirm the page defines familia this broadly.
fact_check_evidence: Latin familia covered everyone under the paterfamilias's authority, including enslaved people; the word comes from famulus, household slave, and could even mean the slaves alone. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_in_ancient_Rome https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pater_familias)

claim: Noble Roman families kept wax masks of their ancestors and carried them in funeral processions.
pre_check: Described by Polybius; confirm the page mentions it or cite another source.
fact_check_evidence: Polybius (Histories 6.53) describes wax likenesses (imagines) of ancestors kept in elite homes and worn by look-alikes in funeral processions; Penn Museum's Expedition magazine summarizes the same practice. (https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.01.0234:book%3D6:chapter%3D53 https://www.penn.museum/sites/expedition/recreating-roman-wax-masks/)

claim: A Roman man’s name usually had three parts, as in Gaius Julius Caesar: a personal name, a clan name and a family branch name.
fact_check_evidence: The tria nomina were praenomen (personal), nomen (gens/clan) and cognomen (family branch); Gaius Julius Caesar is the standard example. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Julius_Caesar_(name) https://www.vroma.org/vromans/bmcmanus/roman_names.html)

claim: Tarquin the Proud, the seventh king, was remembered as a tyrant who ruled by force and ignored the Senate.
fact_check_evidence: Tradition (Livy, Dionysius) portrays Tarquinius Superbus, seventh and last king, as a tyrant who seized power, kept armed guards and bypassed the Senate. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Tarquinius_Superbus https://www.britannica.com/biography/Tarquin-king-of-Rome-534-509-BC)

claim: According to Roman tradition, the assault on the noblewoman Lucretia by the king’s son led to an uprising against the monarchy.
fact_check_evidence: Livy's tradition: Sextus Tarquinius, the king's son, raped Lucretia, sparking the revolt that ended the monarchy (c. 509 BC). Framed as tradition. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucretia https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/rape-lucretia)

claim: According to Roman tradition, the Romans, led by Lucius Junius Brutus, expelled their king in 509 BCE and ended the monarchy.
tested_by: L9 question.ancient_rome.009.q1; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q1; L11 question.ancient_rome.011.q3; L40 question.ancient_rome.040.q3
fact_check_evidence: Brutus is described as semi-legendary; the traditional (Varronian) date is 509 BCE, but the narrative is widely considered largely fictional and the date may be a few years off. (https://www.livius.org/articles/person/junius-brutus-lucius/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overthrow_of_the_Roman_monarchy https://www.britannica.com/topic/Lucius-Junius-Brutus-legendary-Roman)

claim: Afterwards the title rex, king, was so hated in Rome that even its most powerful later leaders avoided it.
fact_check_evidence: After the kings were expelled, rex became a hated title; Caesar publicly refused a crown and Augustus avoided monarchic titles, calling himself princeps. (https://www.unrv.com/articles/why-augustus-refused-to-look-like-a-king.php https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_emperor)

claim: Brutus had the Romans swear never again to allow anyone to be king in Rome.
appears_in: L9 card.ancient_rome.009.c1; L9 card.ancient_rome.009.c3; L40 card.ancient_rome.040.c2
tested_by: L9 question.ancient_rome.009.q1; L10 question.ancient_rome.010.q1; L11 question.ancient_rome.011.q3; L40 question.ancient_rome.040.q3
pre_check: From Livy; confirm the page mentions the oath.
fact_check_evidence: Livy (2.1) reports Brutus made the people swear they would allow no one to reign in Rome. It is Livy's traditional account; historicity is uncertain but the claim reports the tradition. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Junius_Brutus https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overthrow_of_the_Roman_monarchy)

claim: Early Rome’s rise combined a strategic site on the Tiber, Latin villages that merged into a town, strong Etruscan influence, and founding legends Romans used to explain who they were.
fact_check_evidence: Sources describe Rome growing from Latin hilltop villages at a Tiber ford, becoming a city under strong Etruscan influence, with the Romulus and Remus legend serving as its founding story. (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/ancient-rome-founded-twins-romulus-remus-etruscans https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/History/World_History/Western_Civilization_-_A_Concise_History_I_(Brooks)/09:_The_Roman_Republic/9.01:_Roman_Origins)

claim: The word republic comes from the Latin res publica, “the public thing”: a state run by elected officials rather than a king.
tested_by: L11 question.ancient_rome.011.q1; L11 question.ancient_rome.011.q2; L11 question.ancient_rome.011.q3; L12 question.ancient_rome.012.q3
fact_check_evidence: Res publica means 'public thing'; the Republic replaced the kings with elected magistrates, assemblies and a Senate; source of the word republic. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/res-publica https://www.lwvchicago.org/news/democracy-101-politics-roman-republic)

claim: In the Republic, citizens elected officials called magistrates, who held power for a limited term.
tested_by: L11 question.ancient_rome.011.q1; L11 question.ancient_rome.011.q2; L11 question.ancient_rome.011.q3; L12 question.ancient_rome.012.q3
fact_check_evidence: Republican magistrates (consuls, praetors, quaestors, aediles) were elected by citizen assemblies, usually for one-year terms. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_the_Roman_Republic https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul)

claim: Romans called their state SPQR, Senatus Populusque Romanus: “the Senate and People of Rome.”
pre_check: Confirm the page explains SPQR.
fact_check_evidence: SPQR abbreviates Senatus Populusque Romanus, 'the Senate and People of Rome', the formula used on inscriptions, coins and standards to denote the Roman state. (https://www.unrv.com/roman-republic/spqr.php)

claim: Only adult male citizens could vote in the Republic; women, enslaved people and foreigners could not.
pre_check: Confirm the page states the franchise.
fact_check_evidence: Only adult male Roman citizens could vote in the Republic's assemblies; women, slaves and non-citizens were excluded. fact_check_evidence: Hannibal campaigned in Italy from 218 to 203 BC, about 15 years, and left only when recalled to defend Carthage, not driven out. (https://dcc.dickinson.edu/nepos-hannibal-essays/5 https://www.historyworld.net/history/Hannibal/524)

claim: According to tradition, Hannibal’s father made him swear as a boy never to be a friend of Rome.
fact_check_evidence: Polybius reports that Hamilcar had nine-year-old Hannibal swear at an altar never to be a friend of Rome; framed as tradition, which fits scholarly doubts. (http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.01.0234:book%3D3:chapter%3D11 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal)

claim: At Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal surrounded and destroyed a much larger Roman army.
appears_in: L24 card.ancient_rome.024.c1; L24 card.ancient_rome.024.c2; L25 card.ancient_rome.025.c2
tested_by: L24 question.ancient_rome.024.q1; L24 question.ancient_rome.024.q2; L24 question.ancient_rome.024.q3; L29 question.ancient_rome.029.q3; L30 question.ancient_rome.030.q2; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q4
fact_check_evidence: At Cannae in August 216 BC Hannibal's double envelopment surrounded and nearly annihilated a larger Roman and allied army (about 86,000 vs about 50,000). (https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/military-history-and-science/battle-cannae/)

claim: At Cannae, Hannibal let his center fall back while his wings and cavalry closed around the Romans: a double envelopment.
tested_by: L24 question.ancient_rome.024.q1; L24 question.ancient_rome.024.q2; L24 question.ancient_rome.024.q3; L29 question.ancient_rome.029.q3; L30 question.ancient_rome.030.q2; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q4
fact_check_evidence: At Cannae (216 BC) Hannibal's center yielded while African infantry on the wings and his cavalry closed around the Romans, a classic double envelopment. (https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae)

claim: Ancient sources report Roman losses at Cannae in the tens of thousands, one of the worst defeats in Roman history.
fact_check_evidence: Livy reports about 48,000 Roman dead and Polybius about 70,000; Cannae is widely regarded as among Rome's worst defeats. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae)

claim: Cannae is still studied by military historians and officers as the classic example of encirclement.
pre_check: Confirm the page notes its later study.
fact_check_evidence: Cannae is regarded by military historians as the classic example of a victorious double envelopment and has been studied by commanders and military academies ever since. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelopment)

claim: Even after Cannae, Rome refused to make peace with Hannibal.
fact_check_evidence: After Cannae the Senate refused to receive Hannibal's envoy Carthalo, banned talk of peace and refused to ransom prisoners. (https://www.history.com/articles/ancient-romes-darkest-day-the-battle-of-cannae https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae)

claim: Fabius Maximus avoided pitched battles with Hannibal, instead shadowing his army and cutting off his supplies.
fact_check_evidence: Fabius shadowed Hannibal's army, harassed foragers and cut off supplies while refusing pitched battle (the Fabian strategy). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_strategy https://www.britannica.com/biography/Quintus-Fabius-Maximus-Verrucosus)

claim: Fabius’s strategy earned him the nickname Cunctator, “the Delayer,” first as an insult and later as praise.
fact_check_evidence: Romans at first gave Fabius the epithet Cunctator as an insult; after Cannae (216 BC) it became an honorific. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintus_Fabius_Maximus_Verrucosus https://military.wikia.org/wiki/Fabius_Maximus)

claim: A “Fabian strategy” still means wearing down a stronger enemy by avoiding a decisive battle.
fact_check_evidence: A Fabian strategy, named for Fabius Maximus against Hannibal, means avoiding pitched battles and wearing down an opponent by attrition. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_strategy https://www.mountvernon.org/library/digitalhistory/digital-encyclopedia/article/fabian-strategy)

claim: Most of Rome’s Italian allies stayed loyal during Hannibal’s invasion, denying him the reinforcements he needed.
tested_by: L25 question.ancient_rome.025.q2; L25 question.ancient_rome.025.q3; L30 question.ancient_rome.030.q3
fact_check_evidence: Contrary to Hannibal's hopes, most allies (Latium, Umbria, Etruria, Latin colonies) stayed loyal, supplying Rome's manpower; some southern allies did defect after Cannae, but 'most' holds. (https://www.livius.org/articles/person/hannibal-3-barca/ https://warfarehistorynetwork.com/article/rome-avenged-hannibal-in-italy/)

claim: Publius Cornelius Scipio drove the Carthaginians out of Spain and then invaded Africa, forcing Hannibal to return home.
fact_check_evidence: Scipio drove the Carthaginians from Spain (victory at Ilipa, 206 BCE), then invaded Africa, forcing Carthage to recall Hannibal. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Ilipa)

claim: Scipio defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, winning the Second Punic War.
tested_by: L26 question.ancient_rome.026.q1; L26 question.ancient_rome.026.q3; L27 question.ancient_rome.027.q3
fact_check_evidence: At Zama in 202 BC Scipio Africanus decisively defeated Hannibal, leading Carthage to capitulate and ending the Second Punic War. (https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Zama-Roman-Carthaginian-history https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama)

claim: For his victory, Scipio was given the name Africanus.
fact_check_evidence: After defeating Hannibal at Zama in 202 BC, Publius Cornelius Scipio received the cognomen Africanus for his victories in North Africa. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama https://www.worldhistory.org/article/292/the-battle-of-zama---the-beginning-of-roman-conque/)

claim: After Zama, Carthage lost its overseas territories and most of its fleet and paid Rome a huge indemnity.
tested_by: L26 question.ancient_rome.026.q1; L26 question.ancient_rome.026.q3; L27 question.ancient_rome.027.q3
fact_check_evidence: The 201 BC treaty stripped Carthage of overseas territories, limited it to 10 warships, and imposed a 10,000-talent indemnity over 50 years. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthaginian_peace)

claim: In a series of wars against the kingdom of Macedon, ending in 148 BCE, Rome came to control Greece.
fact_check_evidence: The Macedonian Wars (214 to 148 BC), ending with the Fourth War in 148, left Rome in control of Greece; Macedonia became a province in 146. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonian_Wars https://www.britannica.com/event/Macedonian-Wars)

claim: In 196 BCE the Roman general Flamininus proclaimed the Greek cities free, yet Roman influence over them kept growing.
fact_check_evidence: At the Isthmian Games in 196 BC Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks, but Rome kept garrisons and expected obedience, and its influence grew. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Macedonian_War https://www.britannica.com/biography/Titus-Quinctius-Flamininus)

claim: Greek art, literature and philosophy deeply shaped Roman culture; the poet Horace wrote that captive Greece took its fierce conqueror captive.
pre_check: Confirm the page quotes or paraphrases the line.
fact_check_evidence: Horace, Epistles 2.1.156: 'Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit et artes intulit agresti Latio' (captive Greece took her fierce conqueror captive and brought the arts to rustic Latium). (https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Hor.+Ep.+2.1 https://web.sas.upenn.edu/discentes/2020/09/02/graecia-capta-catullus-and-philodemus/)

claim: In 146 BCE Rome destroyed the Greek city of Corinth.
appears_in: L27 card.ancient_rome.027.c4; L28 card.ancient_rome.028.c3; L30 card.ancient_rome.030.c2
fact_check_evidence: In 146 BC the consul Lucius Mummius sacked and destroyed Corinth after the Achaean War. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lucius-Mummius https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Corinth_(146_BC))

claim: The senator Cato the Elder was said to end his speeches with the demand that Carthage must be destroyed.
fact_check_evidence: Ancient sources (e.g. Plutarch) report Cato ended speeches urging Carthage's destruction; the exact Latin phrase is later, but 'was said to' is appropriately hedged. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthago_delenda_est https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Cato_the_Elder)

claim: The Third Punic War (149–146 BCE) ended with Rome capturing and destroying Carthage.
tested_by: L28 question.ancient_rome.028.q2; L28 question.ancient_rome.028.q3; L30 question.ancient_rome.030.q5
fact_check_evidence: The Third Punic War ran 149 to 146 BCE; after a three-year siege Scipio Aemilianus took Carthage, which was burned and razed and its survivors enslaved. (https://www.worldhistory.org/Third_Punic_War/ https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Carthage-146-BCE)

claim: Carthage’s territory became the Roman province of Africa.
tested_by: L28 question.ancient_rome.028.q2; L28 question.ancient_rome.028.q3; L30 question.ancient_rome.030.q5
fact_check_evidence: After Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC at the end of the Third Punic War, Carthage's territory became the Roman province of Africa. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Carthage-146-BCE)

claim: The story that the Romans sowed salt on Carthage’s fields is a much later invention.
pre_check: Confirm the page addresses the salt legend; otherwise find a source that does.
fact_check_evidence: No ancient source mentions salting Carthage. Ridley (1986) traced the claim to modern works, the earliest from about 1930; others traced it back to about 1905. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salting_the_earth https://gwern.net/doc/history/1986-ridley.pdf)

claim: Carthage was later refounded as a Roman colony and became one of the great cities of the empire.
fact_check_evidence: Caesar planned and Augustus carried out the refoundation as Colonia Julia Carthago; it became one of the largest cities of the western empire. (https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Carthage)

claim: In the Republic a legion had roughly 4,000 to 5,000 infantry.
tested_by: L29 question.ancient_rome.029.q1; L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q3; L49 question.ancient_rome.049.q3
pre_check: Figures varied over time; confirm the range.
fact_check_evidence: Polybius gives a manipular legion of 4,200 infantry, raised to 5,000 in emergencies; earlier legions of the 4th century BC are put at 4,200 to 5,000 infantry. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_legion https://www.military-history.us/2011/04/ancient-roman-military-organization-according-to-polybius/)

claim: Republican legions fought in maniples, small flexible units arranged in three lines.
fact_check_evidence: The Republican manipular legion used maniples of about 120 men in three lines (hastati, principes, triarii), giving flexibility. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maniple_(military_unit) https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/hastatii-principes-and-triarii/)

claim: The three lines were the hastati (the youngest men), the principes, and the triarii (the veterans).
fact_check_evidence: The manipular legion's three lines were hastati (youngest), principes (men in their prime) and triarii (veterans). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastati https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/hastatii-principes-and-triarii/)

claim: Legionaries carried a short stabbing sword, the gladius, and heavy throwing javelins called pila.
tested_by: L29 question.ancient_rome.029.q1; L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q3; L49 question.ancient_rome.049.q3
fact_check_evidence: Legionaries threw heavy pila to disrupt the enemy, then closed with the gladius, a short sword used mainly for thrusting. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_military_personal_equipment https://www.unrv.com/military/pilum.php)

claim: The pilum's long, thin iron shank could bend or lodge in a shield, so an enemy could not easily throw it back, though historians debate whether bending was deliberate.
pre_check: Confirm the page describes the bending shank.
fact_check_evidence: The traditional view is that the soft shank bent so it could not be reused, but M. C. Bishop and experimental reconstructions suggest pila rarely bent on impact; bending was not clearly a design aim. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilum)

claim: In the earlier Republic, legionaries were property-owning citizens who supplied their own equipment.
tested_by: L29 question.ancient_rome.029.q1; L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q3; L49 question.ancient_rome.049.q3
fact_check_evidence: Early Republican soldiers were property-owning citizens who met a census qualification and supplied their own arms; the property requirement was dropped around Marius's time. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_reforms https://www.worldatlas.com/ancient-world/how-the-roman-legion-actually-worked.html)

claim: By 146 BCE, after the Punic and Macedonian wars, Rome was the dominant power of the whole Mediterranean.
tested_by: L30 question.ancient_rome.030.q4; L30 question.ancient_rome.030.q5; L75 question.ancient_rome.075.q3
fact_check_evidence: After the Punic and Macedonian wars (Carthage and Corinth fell and Macedonia became a province in 146 BC), Rome held hegemony across the western and eastern Mediterranean. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonian_Wars https://www.britannica.com/event/Macedonian-Wars)

claim: Rome ruled its new overseas lands as provinces run by governors, beginning with Sicily.
fact_check_evidence: Sicily (241 BCE) was Rome's first province; praetors became its regular governors (by c. 227 BCE), and later overseas lands were likewise run as provinces. (https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/province-roman/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilia_(Roman_province))

claim: By the 2nd century BCE, wealthy Romans had built huge estates worked by enslaved people, while many small farmers lost their land.
appears_in: L31 card.ancient_rome.031.c2; L34 card.ancient_rome.034.c2; L34 card.ancient_rome.034.c4
tested_by: L31 question.ancient_rome.031.q1; L31 question.ancient_rome.031.q3; L34 question.ancient_rome.034.q2
fact_check_evidence: By the 2nd century BCE large slave-worked estates (latifundia) displaced many small citizen farmers, the problem Tiberius Gracchus addressed in 133 BC. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latifundium https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracchi_brothers)

claim: Tiberius Gracchus was killed by a mob of senators and their supporters, the first great outbreak of political bloodshed in Rome in centuries.
fact_check_evidence: Tiberius Gracchus was killed in 133 BC by senators and followers led by Scipio Nasica; Plutarch and Cicero call it the first civil bloodshed in Rome since the kings. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius_Gracchus https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Cornelius_Scipio_Nasica_Serapio)

claim: His brother Gaius Gracchus pushed wider reforms, including cheap grain for citizens, and was killed in 121 BCE.
fact_check_evidence: Gaius Gracchus' reforms included a law for subsidized grain sales to citizens; he was killed in 121 BC after the Senate's emergency decree. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Gracchus https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Sempronius-Gracchus)

claim: The deaths of the Gracchi showed that political disputes in Rome could now be settled by violence.
fact_check_evidence: The killings of Tiberius (133 BC) and Gaius Gracchus (121 BC) set a precedent for settling political disputes by violence. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Roman_Republic https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/anc-gracchi-reading/)

claim: In 133 BCE the tribune Tiberius Gracchus proposed giving public land to poor citizens.
fact_check_evidence: As tribune in 133 BCE Tiberius Gracchus proposed enforcing the 500-iugera limit on public land and redistributing reclaimed land to landless poor citizens. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius_Gracchus https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome/The-reform-movement-of-the-Gracchi-133-121-bc)

claim: Gaius Marius was elected consul an unprecedented seven times.
tested_by: L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q1; L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q3; L50 question.ancient_rome.050.q2
fact_check_evidence: Marius was consul seven times (107, 104 to 100, 86 BCE), an unprecedented record in the Republic. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Marius https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Marius)

claim: Marius enrolled poor citizens without property in the army, equipped and paid by the state.
tested_by: L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q1; L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q3; L50 question.ancient_rome.050.q2
fact_check_evidence: In 107 BCE Marius enlisted the capite censi (landless citizens) for the Jugurthine War; since they could not afford arms, the state supplied equipment. Some scholars see this as a one-off measure rather than a sweeping reform. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_reforms https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1598/marian-reforms/)

claim: Marius defeated the invading Cimbri and Teutones, Germanic peoples, in 102 and 101 BCE.
tested_by: L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q1; L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q3; L50 question.ancient_rome.050.q2
fact_check_evidence: Marius destroyed the Teutones at Aquae Sextiae in 102 BC and the Cimbri at Vercellae in 101 BC. (https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/battles_aquae_sextiae.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vercellae)

claim: Marius made the silver eagle, the aquila, the standard of every legion.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions the eagle standard.
fact_check_evidence: Pliny (NH 10.16) says Marius in 104 BCE kept the eagle alone as the legionary standard; Sallust mentions Marius's silver eagle from the Cimbric War, and aquilae were typically silver or bronze. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquila_(Roman) https://rosscowan.substack.com/p/catilines-eagle)

claim: After Marius, soldiers increasingly looked to their general, not the Senate, for pay and for land when they retired.
appears_in: L32 card.ancient_rome.032.c3; L33 card.ancient_rome.033.c2; L33 card.ancient_rome.033.c4; L99 card.ancient_rome.099.c3
tested_by: L32 question.ancient_rome.032.q2; L38 question.ancient_rome.038.q3; L40 question.ancient_rome.040.q4; L50 question.ancient_rome.050.q6; L55 question.ancient_rome.055.q3; L99 question.ancient_rome.099.q2; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q9
fact_check_evidence: After Marius's reforms, landless recruits depended on their generals for booty and land on discharge, shifting loyalty from the Senate to commanders. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_reforms https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1598/marian-reforms/)

claim: Sulla and Marius, and their supporters, fought a civil war for control of Rome.
tested_by: L33 question.ancient_rome.033.q1; L35 question.ancient_rome.035.q3; L39 question.ancient_rome.039.q3; L40 question.ancient_rome.040.q2; L50 question.ancient_rome.050.q7
fact_check_evidence: Sulla marched on Rome in 88 BC against Marius and Sulpicius; war resumed 83 to 82 BC against Marius' faction. (https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/wars_sullas_first_civil_war.html https://www.britannica.com/biography/Sulla)

claim: Sulla took the dictatorship with no time limit, reformed the constitution to strengthen the Senate, and then retired.
fact_check_evidence: Sulla was made dictator for writing laws with no time limit set, reformed the constitution to restore Senate primacy, resigned in 80/79 BC and retired to Campania. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_reforms_of_Sulla https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1481/sullas-reforms-as-dictator/)

claim: As dictator, Sulla published proscription lists of enemies who could be killed and their property seized.
fact_check_evidence: Sulla published proscription lists of enemies; those listed could be killed with rewards to the killers and their property was confiscated. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulla's_proscription https://www.britannica.com/biography/Sulla)

claim: In 88 BCE Sulla marched his army on Rome itself, something no Roman general had done before.
appears_in: L33 card.ancient_rome.033.c1; L33 card.ancient_rome.033.c2; L33 card.ancient_rome.033.c4; L50 card.ancient_rome.050.c3
tested_by: L33 question.ancient_rome.033.q1; L35 question.ancient_rome.035.q3; L39 question.ancient_rome.039.q3; L40 question.ancient_rome.040.q2; L50 question.ancient_rome.050.q7
fact_check_evidence: Sulla's 88 BCE march on Rome is described as the first time a Roman general led his army against the city, entering the pomerium under arms. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Rome_(88_BC) https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2146/sullas-march-on-rome/)

claim: In 73 BCE Spartacus, a Thracian gladiator, escaped from a gladiator school at Capua and began a slave revolt.
tested_by: L34 question.ancient_rome.034.q1; L34 question.ancient_rome.034.q2; L62 question.ancient_rome.062.q3; L64 question.ancient_rome.064.q3
fact_check_evidence: In 73 BCE the Thracian gladiator Spartacus escaped a gladiatorial school at Capua with about 70 others, starting the Third Servile War. (https://www.history.com/articles/spartacus-slave-revolt-ancient-rome https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spartacus)

claim: The rebel army of escaped slaves grew to tens of thousands and defeated several Roman forces.
tested_by: L34 question.ancient_rome.034.q1; L34 question.ancient_rome.034.q2; L62 question.ancient_rome.062.q3; L64 question.ancient_rome.064.q3
fact_check_evidence: Spartacus's force grew to roughly 70,000 or more (some sources say up to 120,000) and defeated several Roman armies, including consular ones. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Spartacus-Roman-gladiator https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Servile_War)

claim: Marcus Crassus crushed the revolt of Spartacus in 71 BCE.
fact_check_evidence: The Third Servile War ended in 71 BC when Crassus defeated Spartacus' army; Spartacus was killed and survivors were crucified along the Appian Way. (https://www.britannica.com/event/Gladiatorial-War https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Servile_War)

claim: Marcus Crassus crushed the revolt of Spartacus in 71 BCE.
fact_check_evidence: The Third Servile War ended in 71 BC when Crassus defeated Spartacus' army; Spartacus was killed and survivors were crucified along the Appian Way. (https://www.britannica.com/event/Gladiatorial-War https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Servile_War)

claim: Some 6,000 captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way.
pre_check: The figure comes from Appian; confirm the page gives it.
fact_check_evidence: Following Appian, standard accounts say Crassus had 6,000 captured followers of Spartacus crucified along the Appian Way between Capua and Rome in 71 BCE. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Servile_War https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spartacus)

claim: Spartacus later became a symbol of resistance to oppression.
fact_check_evidence: Spartacus became a symbol for later revolutionaries and resistance movements, praised by Marx and adopted by the German Spartacist League. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spartacus https://links.org.au/spartacus-rebel-or-proto-communist)

claim: Pompey first rose to fame as a young commander fighting for Sulla.
fact_check_evidence: In 83 BCE the 23-year-old Pompey raised three legions and joined Sulla, rising to prominence as his commander in the civil war and in Sicily and Africa. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/anc-pompey-reading/)

claim: Pompey received extraordinary commands that gave him power over huge areas for years at a time.
fact_check_evidence: Lex Gabinia (67 BCE) gave Pompey 3 years' command over the Mediterranean and coasts; lex Manilia (66 BCE) the war in the East. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Gabinia_de_piratis_persequendis https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Manilia)

claim: In 67 BCE Pompey cleared the Mediterranean of pirates in about three months.
fact_check_evidence: Under the Lex Gabinia of 67 BCE Pompey received a three-year command but cleared the pirates in about three months. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey's_campaign_against_the_pirates https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/67_BC)

claim: Pompey defeated King Mithridates and reorganized the eastern Mediterranean, making Syria a Roman province and capturing Jerusalem in 63 BCE.
fact_check_evidence: After ending the Third Mithridatic War, Pompey annexed Syria as a province (64 BCE) and took Jerusalem in 63 BCE. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Syria https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(63_BC))

claim: Pompey was hailed as Magnus, “the Great,” by his troops and by Sulla, and he used the name. It echoed Alexander the Great, whom Pompey admired and imitated.
fact_check_evidence: Sources say Pompey's troops and Sulla hailed him Magnus around 81 BCE (possibly ironically); the name echoed Alexander, whom Pompey admired and imitated. Not simply self-chosen in imitation. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/pompey-great/)

claim: Cicero was a “new man,” the first in his family to reach the Senate, and became Rome’s greatest orator.
fact_check_evidence: Cicero was a novus homo, the first in his family to enter the Senate and later reach the consulship; he is widely regarded as Rome's greatest orator. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novus_homo https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero)

claim: Cicero was elected consul for 63 BCE.
tested_by: L36 question.ancient_rome.036.q1; L36 question.ancient_rome.036.q2; L36 question.ancient_rome.036.q3
fact_check_evidence: Cicero won the consular election in 64 BC and served as consul in 63 BC with Gaius Antonius Hybrida. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catilinarian_conspiracy https://www.worldhistory.org/article/861/cicero--the-catiline-conspiracy/)
