fact_check_evidence: Virgil's Aeneid is a twelve-book epic closely modeled on Homer: books 1 to 6 echo the Odyssey, books 7 to 12 the Iliad. (https://www.britannica.com/question/How-is-the-Aeneid-related-to-Homers-epics https://www.worldhistory.org/The_Aeneid/)

claim: The Aeneid tells how the Trojan prince Aeneas escaped burning Troy and, guided by fate, came to Italy, where his descendants would found Rome.
fact_check_evidence: Virgil's Aeneid tells how Aeneas fled burning Troy and, driven by destiny, reached Italy; his son Ascanius founded Alba Longa, the line leading to Romulus and Remus. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid https://www.worldhistory.org/Aeneas/)

claim: The Julian family, including Caesar and Augustus, claimed descent from Aeneas through his son Iulus.
fact_check_evidence: The gens Iulia claimed descent from Aeneas's son Ascanius, also called Iulus, and through Aeneas from Venus; Julius Caesar and the Julio-Claudians used this genealogy. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_gens https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascanius)

claim: Aeneas is famous for pietas, dutiful devotion to the gods, his family and his country.
fact_check_evidence: Pietas means duty and devotion to the gods, family and country; Virgil repeatedly calls him 'pius Aeneas'. (https://www.open.edu/openlearn/history-the-arts/introducing-virgils-aeneid/content-section-3.3 https://www.litcharts.com/lit/the-aeneid/themes/piety)

claim: Virgil died before finishing the Aeneid and asked for it to be burned; Augustus had it published instead.
fact_check_evidence: Suetonius and EBSCO: Virgil died in 19 BC wanting the unfinished Aeneid burned; Augustus had his executors Varius and Tucca publish it with minimal changes. (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Suetonius/de_Poetis/Vergil*.html https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/roman-poet-vergil-dies)

claim: In 46 BCE Julius Caesar introduced the Julian calendar, with 365 days and a leap day every fourth year, an average of 365.25 days.
fact_check_evidence: Caesar introduced the Julian calendar in 46 BC (effective 45 BC): 365 days with a leap day every fourth year, averaging 365.25 days. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/julian-calendar/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/46_BC)

claim: Caesar based the calendar reform on the advice of the astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria.
fact_check_evidence: Pliny (NH 18.210 to 212) says Caesar consulted Sosigenes for the calendar; Britannica calls him Sosigenes of Alexandria (some note no ancient source gives 'of Alexandria'). (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Sosigenes-of-Alexandria https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sosigenes_(astronomer))

claim: The Roman year once began in March, so the month Quintilis meant “fifth month.”
fact_check_evidence: Quintilis means 'fifth month', its position in the early Roman calendar that began with March. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintilis https://www.dictionary.com/articles/july)

claim: The Julian year was about 11 minutes too long and drifted against the seasons; in 1582 Pope Gregory XIII replaced it with the Gregorian calendar used today.
fact_check_evidence: The Julian year (365.25 days) was about 11 minutes longer than the tropical year; Gregory XIII's 1582 bull Inter gravissimas introduced the Gregorian calendar. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/manuscriptsandspecialcollections/researchguidance/datingdocuments/juliangregorian.aspx)

claim: The Julian year was about 11 minutes too long and drifted against the seasons; in 1582 Pope Gregory XIII replaced it with the Gregorian calendar used today.
fact_check_evidence: The Julian year (365.25 days) was about 11 minutes longer than the tropical year; Gregory XIII's 1582 bull Inter gravissimas introduced the Gregorian calendar. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/manuscriptsandspecialcollections/researchguidance/datingdocuments/juliangregorian.aspx)

claim: Quintilis was renamed Julius, our July, in honor of Julius Caesar.
fact_check_evidence: In 44 BC Quintilis, Caesar's birth month, was renamed Julius in his honor, becoming July. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintilis https://www.library.illinois.edu/hpnl/blog/july-blog-post-julius-caesars-month/)

claim: The month Sextilis was renamed Augustus, our August, in honor of Augustus in 8 BCE.
fact_check_evidence: Sextilis was renamed Augustus in 8 BC by a senatus consultum honoring the emperor, citing events of his career that fell in that month. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextilis https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8_BC)

claim: In 9 CE, Germanic warriors led by Arminius destroyed three Roman legions under the governor Varus in the Teutoburg Forest.
tested_by: L49 question.ancient_rome.049.q1; L49 question.ancient_rome.049.q3; L89 question.ancient_rome.089.q3
fact_check_evidence: In September 9 CE a Germanic coalition under Arminius destroyed Legions XVII, XVIII and XIX under the governor Publius Quinctilius Varus. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/battle-teutoburg-forest/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Teutoburg_Forest)

claim: Arminius had served with the Roman army and was trusted by Varus, whom he led into an ambush.
tested_by: L49 question.ancient_rome.049.q1; L49 question.ancient_rome.049.q3; L89 question.ancient_rome.089.q3
fact_check_evidence: Arminius commanded a Germanic auxiliary unit in the Roman army, was trusted by Varus as an adviser, and led him into the Teutoburg ambush in 9 CE. (https://www.worldhistory.org/Arminius/ https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/biography/arminius/)

claim: After the disaster, Rome gave up plans to conquer Germany east of the Rhine, which became a lasting frontier.
fact_check_evidence: After Varus's defeat Augustus abandoned plans to extend the frontier to the Elbe; the Rhine (with the Danube) remained the border. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Teutoburg_Forest https://warfarehistorynetwork.com/article/teutonic-fury/)

claim: Archaeologists believe the battlefield lies near Kalkriese in Germany, where Roman weapons and coins have been found.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions Kalkriese.
fact_check_evidence: Excavations at Kalkriese near Osnabrueck have yielded thousands of Roman military finds and over 1,500 coins (some countermarked VAR); most scholars identify it as a site of the Varus battle. (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/teutoburg-forest-9-ce/kalkriese/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalkriese)

claim: According to the historian Suetonius, Augustus cried out, “Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!”
pre_check: The quotation is from Suetonius; confirm the page gives it.
fact_check_evidence: Suetonius (Augustus 23) says Augustus beat his head against a door crying 'Quintili Vare, legiones redde!' ('Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!'). (https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0132%3Alife%3Daug.%3Achapter%3D23)

claim: The change from Republic to Empire kept republican forms, such as the Senate and the consuls, while real power passed to one man.
fact_check_evidence: Under Augustus the Senate, consuls and assemblies continued, but real control of armies, provinces and money lay with the princeps. (https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2363/the-principate-of-augustus/ https://brewminate.com/emperor-in-disguise-how-augustus-ended-the-roman-republic-while-pretending-to-save-it/)

claim: The word emperor comes from imperator, a title Roman soldiers gave to a victorious commander.
fact_check_evidence: Imperator meant commander; troops acclaimed a victorious general as imperator, and the title later came to denote the emperor, giving English 'emperor'. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperator https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803095959143)

claim: Augustus had no surviving son, and adopted his stepson Tiberius as heir after other chosen successors died.
tested_by: L51 question.ancient_rome.051.q1; L51 question.ancient_rome.051.q2; L51 question.ancient_rome.051.q3; L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q4; L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q3
fact_check_evidence: Augustus had no son of his own; his adopted heirs Lucius (d. 2 CE) and Gaius (d. 4 CE) died, and he adopted stepson Tiberius in 4 CE. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius https://familyandsuccession.omeka.net/exhibits/show/family-succession/augustus-gaius-lucius)

claim: Tiberius became emperor on Augustus’ death in 14 CE and ruled until 37 CE.
tested_by: L51 question.ancient_rome.051.q1; L51 question.ancient_rome.051.q2; L51 question.ancient_rome.051.q3; L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q4; L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q3
fact_check_evidence: Tiberius succeeded his stepfather and adoptive father Augustus in AD 14 and reigned until his death in March AD 37. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius)

claim: Rome never had a fixed law of succession; each emperor had to choose an heir, often by adoption.
tested_by: L51 question.ancient_rome.051.q1; L51 question.ancient_rome.051.q2; L51 question.ancient_rome.051.q3; L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q4; L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q3
fact_check_evidence: There was no written law of imperial succession; emperors designated heirs, frequently by adoption (Augustus-Tiberius, Claudius-Nero, the Nerva-Antonines). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nerva%E2%80%93Antonine_dynasty https://www.unrv.com/articles/how-roman-emperors-chose-their-heirs.php)

claim: In his later years Tiberius withdrew to the island of Capri and ruled from there.
fact_check_evidence: Tiberius withdrew to Capri in 26/27 CE and governed from the island, largely through Sejanus and correspondence, until his death in 37 CE. (https://www.unrv.com/articles/tiberius-on-capri-retirement-rumor-imperial-power.php https://blog.oup.com/2014/11/roman-emperor-tiberius-capri-suetonius/)

claim: While Tiberius was away, Sejanus, commander of the Praetorian Guard, grew powerful until Tiberius had him executed in 31 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Sejanus, Praetorian prefect, ran affairs in Rome after Tiberius withdrew to Capri in 26 CE; on Tiberius' orders he was arrested and executed on 18 October 31 CE. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sejanus https://www.executedtoday.com/2008/10/18/31-sejanus-captain-of-the-praetorian-guard/)

claim: The Praetorian Guard was the emperor’s bodyguard, stationed in Rome itself.
fact_check_evidence: The Praetorian Guard protected the emperor; Sejanus concentrated it in the Castra Praetoria at Rome in 23 AD. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castra_Praetoria https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/praetorian-guard/)

claim: Gaius, known as Caligula, became emperor in 37 CE and was murdered by officers of the Praetorian Guard in 41 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Caligula became emperor in AD 37 and was assassinated on 24 January AD 41 by a plot led by the Praetorian officer Cassius Chaerea. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassius_Chaerea https://www.thecollector.com/palatine-plot-death-emperor-caligula/)

claim: Caligula means “little boot,” a nickname soldiers gave him as a child, when he wore a small soldier’s uniform in his father’s camp.
fact_check_evidence: Caligula ('little boots', from caliga) was a childhood nickname from his father Germanicus's soldiers, as he wore a miniature soldier's outfit in camp. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula https://fitzmuseum.cam.ac.uk/explore-our-collection/highlights/GR1111937)

claim: Caligula was popular at first, but his rule soon became autocratic and extravagant.
fact_check_evidence: Caligula was initially popular (tax cuts, bonuses, games), but his rule soon became erratic, autocratic and extravagant, emptying the treasury. (https://www.worldhistory.org/Caligula/ https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/caligula)

claim: The story that Caligula planned to make his horse a consul may be a joke or an exaggeration.
pre_check: Confirm the page discusses the horse story.
fact_check_evidence: Suetonius and Dio say only that Caligula planned or promised to make Incitatus consul, and it never happened; modern historians read it as a joke or insult aimed at the Senate, or as hostile exaggeration. (https://theconversation.com/mythbusting-ancient-rome-caligulas-horse-75837 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incitatus)

claim: Most accounts of Caligula come from later writers hostile to him, so historians treat the wildest stories with caution.
appears_in: L52 card.ancient_rome.052.c1; L52 card.ancient_rome.052.c3; L98 card.ancient_rome.098.c2
fact_check_evidence: Main sources (Suetonius, Cassius Dio, Seneca, Philo) are later or hostile; historians such as Barrett urge caution about lurid stories. (https://www.thecollector.com/what-are-the-principal-sources-of-emperor-caligulas-reign/ https://hekint.org/2025/09/05/caligula-revisited/)

claim: After Caligula’s murder, the Praetorian Guard made his uncle Claudius emperor in 41 CE.
fact_check_evidence: After Caligula's assassination in AD 41, his uncle Claudius was proclaimed emperor by the Praetorian Guard. (https://www.thecollector.com/palatine-plot-death-emperor-caligula/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassius_Chaerea)

claim: Claudius had a limp and a stammer, and his family kept him out of public life; he was a scholar who wrote histories, now lost.
fact_check_evidence: Claudius limped and stammered; Augustus kept him out of public life. He wrote histories of the Etruscans and Carthaginians, none of which survive. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/claudius https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrrhenika)

claim: In 43 CE Claudius launched the invasion of Britain, which became a Roman province.
appears_in: L53 card.ancient_rome.053.c1; L53 card.ancient_rome.053.c3; L53 card.ancient_rome.053.c4
fact_check_evidence: Claudius' invasion under Aulus Plautius landed in AD 43; after Camulodunum submitted, the province of Britannia was established. (https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/learn/story-of-england/romans/invasion/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_conquest_of_Britain)

claim: In about 60 CE Boudica, queen of the Iceni, led a revolt in Britain that burned London before the Romans crushed it.
fact_check_evidence: Boudica's Iceni revolt, c. AD 60 to 61, burned Londinium, Camulodunum and Verulamium before Suetonius Paulinus crushed it. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boudican_revolt https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/boudica-britain-revolt-against-rome)

claim: Claudius relied on freedmen, formerly enslaved people, as powerful officials.
fact_check_evidence: Claudius put freedmen such as Narcissus, Pallas and Callistus in charge of government departments, where they became rich and powerful. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius_Claudius_Narcissus https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pallas_(freedman))

claim: Nero, Claudius’ adopted son, became emperor in 54 CE at the age of 16.
fact_check_evidence: Sources state Claudius died in 54 CE and his adopted son Nero, born 15 Dec 37 CE, became emperor at 16. (https://www.worldhistory.org/Nero/ https://www.britannica.com/biography/Nero-Roman-emperor)

claim: In 64 CE a great fire burned in Rome for six days; three of the city’s 14 districts were destroyed and seven more badly damaged.
tested_by: L54 question.ancient_rome.054.q1; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q3; L84 question.ancient_rome.084.q3
pre_check: Confirm the district counts.
fact_check_evidence: Tacitus (Annals 15.38-41) says the fire raged six days before being checked (it then flared up again briefly); of Rome's 14 regions, 3 were levelled, 7 left with a few ruined houses, 4 untouched. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_Rome https://dcc.dickinson.edu/tacitus-annals/introduction/annals-outline/annals-38-41-outline)

claim: According to the historian Tacitus, Nero blamed the Christians in Rome for the fire and had many of them executed, though a few scholars question this account.
tested_by: L54 question.ancient_rome.054.q1; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q3; L84 question.ancient_rome.084.q3
fact_check_evidence: The account comes solely from Tacitus, written decades later. Most historians accept it, but some (notably Brent Shaw) question whether Christians were targeted as a group or linked to the fire. (https://www.livius.org/sources/content/tacitus/tacitus-on-the-christians/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_Rome)

claim: Nero built a vast palace, the Golden House, on land cleared by the fire.
tested_by: L54 question.ancient_rome.054.q1; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q3; L84 question.ancient_rome.084.q3
fact_check_evidence: After the fire of 64 CE Nero took over a large area cleared by the fire (plus other land) for the Domus Aurea, built c. 64 to 68 CE. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Golden-House-of-Nero https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domus_Aurea)

claim: The story that Nero fiddled while Rome burned is a later legend: the fiddle did not yet exist, and Tacitus says Nero was away at Antium when the fire began.
fact_check_evidence: The violin did not exist until about the 16th century; Tacitus says Nero was at Antium when the fire broke out and reports the singing story only as rumour. (https://talesoftimesforgotten.com/2017/11/26/no-emperor-nero-did-not-play-the-fiddle-as-rome-burned/ https://www.history.com/articles/did-nero-really-fiddle-while-rome-burned)

claim: The story that Nero fiddled while Rome burned is a later legend: the fiddle did not yet exist, and Tacitus says Nero was away at Antium when the fire began.
fact_check_evidence: The violin did not exist until about the 16th century; Tacitus says Nero was at Antium when the fire broke out and reports the singing story only as rumour. (https://talesoftimesforgotten.com/2017/11/26/no-emperor-nero-did-not-play-the-fiddle-as-rome-burned/ https://www.history.com/articles/did-nero-really-fiddle-while-rome-burned)

claim: Facing revolt, Nero took his own life in 68 CE, ending the Julio-Claudian dynasty, the family line of Augustus.
fact_check_evidence: Nero killed himself on 9 June 68 CE after the Senate declared him a public enemy amid revolts; his death ended the Julio-Claudian dynasty begun by Augustus. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio-Claudian_dynasty https://www.worldhistory.org/Nero/)

claim: In 69 CE, the Year of the Four Emperors, Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian each held power in turn.
tested_by: L55 question.ancient_rome.055.q2; L55 question.ancient_rome.055.q3; L81 question.ancient_rome.081.q3
fact_check_evidence: In 69 Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian ruled in succession; Galba was killed in January, Otho died in April, Vitellius fell in December, and Vespasian prevailed. (https://www.worldhistory.org/Year_of_the_Four_Emperors/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Four_Emperors)

claim: Each claimant in 69 CE was backed by an army, showing that the legions could make and unmake emperors.
tested_by: L55 question.ancient_rome.055.q2; L55 question.ancient_rome.055.q3; L81 question.ancient_rome.081.q3
fact_check_evidence: In 69 CE Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian each rose with military backing; Tacitus said the year revealed that an emperor could be made outside Rome by the armies. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/year-four-emperors https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Four_Emperors)

claim: Vespasian, a general commanding in Judaea, won the civil war and founded the Flavian dynasty.
fact_check_evidence: Vespasian, commanding against the Jewish revolt in Judaea, was proclaimed emperor in 69 CE, won the civil war and founded the Flavian dynasty. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vespasian https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-worldhistory/chapter/the-flavian-dynasty/)

claim: The historian Tacitus wrote that the fall of Nero in 68 CE revealed a secret of empire: an emperor could be made somewhere other than Rome.
pre_check: Confirm the page quotes Tacitus.
fact_check_evidence: Tacitus, Histories 1.4, ties the revealed 'secret of empire' (an emperor could be made elsewhere than Rome) to the end of Nero in 68 CE and Galba's proclamation by the armies, not to 69 CE itself. (https://www.latin.it/autore/tacito/historiae/!01!liber_i https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histories_(Tacitus))

claim: Vespasian came from a family of modest rank, not the old Roman nobility.
fact_check_evidence: Vespasian came from an undistinguished Sabine equestrian family (his father was a tax collector and moneylender), not the senatorial nobility. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vespasian)

claim: In 70 CE Vespasian’s son Titus captured Jerusalem and destroyed its Temple.
fact_check_evidence: In 70 AD Titus, son of Vespasian, besieged and captured Jerusalem, and the Second Temple was destroyed. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(70_CE) https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1993/the-siege-of-jerusalem-in-70-ce/)

claim: Titus succeeded Vespasian and was followed by his brother Domitian, whose harsh rule ended with his murder in 96 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Domitian succeeded his brother Titus in 81 and was assassinated by court officials on 18 September 96. His reign is widely described as autocratic. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domitian https://www.britannica.com/summary/Domitian)

claim: Vespasian began the Colosseum, and his son Titus opened it in 80 CE.
tested_by: L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q1; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q2; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q3; L57 question.ancient_rome.057.q3; L65 question.ancient_rome.065.q3
fact_check_evidence: Construction began under Vespasian around AD 70 to 72; his son Titus completed and opened it in AD 80 with 100 days of games. (https://www.history.com/articles/colosseum https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum)

claim: The games held to open the Colosseum lasted 100 days.
tested_by: L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q1; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q2; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q3; L57 question.ancient_rome.057.q3; L65 question.ancient_rome.065.q3
pre_check: Confirm the page gives the 100 days.
fact_check_evidence: Titus opened the Flavian Amphitheatre in AD 80 with games that ancient sources (Cassius Dio) say lasted 100 days. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inaugural_games_of_the_Colosseum https://www.thecollector.com/inaugural-games-colosseum/)

claim: The Colosseum could hold about 50,000 spectators.
tested_by: L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q1; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q2; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q3; L57 question.ancient_rome.057.q3; L65 question.ancient_rome.065.q3
fact_check_evidence: Standard references give seating for about 50,000 spectators (some estimates run higher), consistent with 'about 50,000'. (https://www.history.com/articles/colosseum https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum)

claim: The Colosseum was built on the site of a lake in the grounds of Nero’s Golden House, giving the land back to public use.
tested_by: L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q1; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q2; L56 question.ancient_rome.056.q3; L57 question.ancient_rome.057.q3; L65 question.ancient_rome.065.q3
fact_check_evidence: The Colosseum stands on the site of the artificial lake of Nero's Domus Aurea; Vespasian's arena returned the land to public use. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domus_Aurea https://www.britannica.com/topic/Golden-House-of-Nero)

claim: The Colosseum is also known as the Flavian Amphitheatre, after the dynasty that built it, though Romans mostly just called it the amphitheatre. The name Colosseum came later, probably from a colossal statue of Nero nearby.
fact_check_evidence: The Colosseum name likely comes from the nearby Colossus of Nero. But there is no evidence Flavian Amphitheatre (Amphitheatrum Flavium) was used in antiquity; the building was simply called amphitheatrum, and the Flavian name was applied later. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colossus_of_Nero)

claim: Titus was emperor when Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Titus became emperor on 24 June 79 CE after Vespasian died; Vesuvius erupted later that year (traditionally 24 August 79 CE) and Titus led relief efforts. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titus https://pompeiiarchaeologicalpark.com/emperor-titus-and-romes-response-to-the-disaster-of-pompeii/)

claim: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum.
fact_check_evidence: The 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius buried Pompeii under 4 to 6 m of ash and pumice and Herculaneum under deeper volcanic deposits. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eruption_of_Mount_Vesuvius_in_79_AD https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/august-24/vesuvius-erupts)

claim: Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters to the historian Tacitus; his uncle, Pliny the Elder, died trying to rescue people.
fact_check_evidence: Pliny the Younger wrote two letters to Tacitus about the 79 CE eruption; his uncle Pliny the Elder died on a rescue expedition from Misenum. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Younger https://cmuntz.hosted.uark.edu/texts/pliny-the-younger/the-eruption-of-vesuvius.html)

claim: Pompeii was buried under several meters of ash and pumice, which preserved buildings, paintings and everyday objects.
fact_check_evidence: Pompeii was buried under roughly 4 to 6 m of ash and pumice in AD 79, preserving buildings, frescoes and objects. (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/pompeii)

claim: Pompeii’s walls preserve painted notices and scratched graffiti, including election slogans.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions graffiti or election notices.
fact_check_evidence: Pompeii preserves more than 2,600 painted electoral notices (programmata) plus many scratched graffiti. (https://www.worldhistory.org/article/467/pompeii-graffiti-signs--electoral-notices/ https://www.pompeionline.net/en/archaeological-park-of-pompeii/pompeian-graffiti)

claim: In the 1800s, excavators poured plaster into hollows left in the ash by victims’ bodies, making casts of their final positions.
fact_check_evidence: In 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli had plaster poured into cavities left in the hardened ash by decomposed bodies, producing casts of victims' final poses. (http://www.thehistoryblog.com/archives/36706 https://pompeiisites.org/en/pompeii-map/analysis/the-casts/)

claim: Pompeii gives historians a rare snapshot of ordinary Roman town life.
fact_check_evidence: Buried in 79 CE, Pompeii preserves shops, homes, graffiti and food counters, giving a rare snapshot of ordinary life in a Roman town. (https://www.historyhit.com/pompeii-a-snapshot-of-ancient-roman-life/)

claim: Trajan, born in Spain, was the first emperor from outside Italy; he ruled from 98 to 117 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Trajan was born at Italica in Hispania and is described as the first emperor born outside Italy; he reigned 98 to 117 CE. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Trajan https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/trajan)

claim: The Senate gave Trajan the title Optimus, “the best.”
fact_check_evidence: The Senate granted Trajan the title Optimus (optimus princeps, 'the best'), officially around 114 CE. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/trajan/)

claim: Trajan conquered Dacia, roughly modern Romania, in two wars ending in 106 CE.
tested_by: L58 question.ancient_rome.058.q2; L58 question.ancient_rome.058.q3; L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q2; L68 question.ancient_rome.068.q3
fact_check_evidence: Trajan fought two Dacian Wars (101 to 102 and 105 to 106); Sarmizegetusa fell in 106 and Dacia, roughly modern Romania, became a province. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacian_Wars https://www.britannica.com/biography/Trajan/Military-campaigns)

claim: Trajan’s Column in Rome shows the Dacian wars in a spiral band of carvings winding from base to top.
fact_check_evidence: A continuous spiral relief winds 23 times from base to top, depicting both Dacian wars (101-102 and 105-106 CE). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan%27s_Column https://www.nationalgeographic.com/trajan-column/)

claim: Under Trajan the empire reached its greatest extent, in 117 CE, after he conquered lands as far as Mesopotamia.

claim: Hadrian, Trajan’s successor, ruled from 117 to 138 CE and gave up some of Trajan’s eastern conquests.

claim: Hadrian spent much of his reign traveling through the provinces, inspecting the armies and frontiers.
tested_by: L59 question.ancient_rome.059.q2; L59 question.ancient_rome.059.q3; L74 question.ancient_rome.074.q3
fact_check_evidence: Hadrian spent roughly half his 21-year reign touring the provinces, inspecting troops, forts and frontier defenses. (https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/hadrians-wall/hadrians-wall-history-and-stories/hadrian/ https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hadrian/Policies-as-emperor)

claim: Hadrian’s Wall, begun in 122 CE, ran about 118 km across northern Britain.
fact_check_evidence: Hadrian's Wall was begun in AD 122; its length was 80 Roman miles, about 73 modern miles or 117 to 118 km, across northern Britain. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrian%27s_Wall https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/hadrians-wall/hadrians-wall-history-and-stories/history/)

claim: Hadrian loved Greek culture and was the first emperor regularly portrayed with a full beard, in the Greek style.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions the beard.
fact_check_evidence: Hadrian was a philhellene and made the beard a permanent imperial fashion, but Nero, Titus and Domitian were occasionally shown bearded (mostly on coins), so 'first to wear' is overstated. (https://publications.artic.edu/roman/api/epub/480/493/print_view https://www.dailyartmagazine.com/identify-roman-emperor-by-beard/)

claim: Hadrian’s Wall had small forts about every Roman mile, and larger forts along its length.
fact_check_evidence: The Wall had about 80 milecastles, one roughly every Roman mile, with turrets between and larger forts such as Housesteads and Chesters. (https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/faqs-hadrians-wall/ https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/hadrians-wall/hadrians-wall-history-and-stories/history/description/)

claim: Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, who ruled from 96 to 180 CE, are known as the Five Good Emperors.
tested_by: L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q3; L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q5; L94 question.ancient_rome.094.q3
fact_check_evidence: The Five Good Emperors are Nerva (96 to 98), Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius (161 to 180). (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Five-Good-Emperors https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Emperors)

claim: None of the first four Good Emperors left a surviving son, so each passed power to an adopted adult heir, though even ancient writers doubted that Trajan really adopted Hadrian before he died.
tested_by: L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q3; L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q5; L94 question.ancient_rome.094.q3
fact_check_evidence: Successions were by adoption, but these emperors had no surviving sons (e.g. Antoninus's only surviving child was a daughter), and Trajan's deathbed adoption of Hadrian was doubted in antiquity, with Plotina suspected of arranging it. (https://followinghadrian.com/2013/08/09/the-death-of-trajan-and-ascension-of-hadrian/ https://blogs.nottingham.ac.uk/mintimperials/2015/02/25/1877-years-ago-today-hadrian-adopted-pius-on-the-proviso-pius-adopted-marcus-aurelius-and-lucius-verus/ https://www.encyclopedia.com/women/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/plotina-d-122)

claim: The historian Edward Gibbon called this era the time when the human race was most happy and prosperous.
tested_by: L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q3; L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q5; L94 question.ancient_rome.094.q3
pre_check: Confirm one page gives Gibbon’s judgment.
fact_check_evidence: In Decline and Fall ch. 3 Gibbon named the period from Domitian's death to Commodus' accession (the Five Good Emperors) as when 'the condition of the human race was most happy and prosperous'. (https://academickids.com/encyclopedia/index.php/Five_Good_Emperors)

claim: The historian Edward Gibbon called this era the time when the human race was most happy and prosperous.
tested_by: L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q3; L60 question.ancient_rome.060.q5; L94 question.ancient_rome.094.q3

claim: Marcus Aurelius, a Stoic philosopher, wrote his private reflections, the Meditations, while on campaign.
fact_check_evidence: The Meditations, private Stoic notes addressed to himself, were largely written in the 170s during the Danube campaigns (Marcomannic Wars). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations https://www.britannica.com/topic/Meditations-by-Marcus-Aurelius)

claim: A deadly epidemic, the Antonine Plague, swept the empire from about 165 CE.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions the plague.
fact_check_evidence: The Antonine Plague (Plague of Galen), probably smallpox, broke out in 165 CE under Marcus Aurelius and spread across the empire until about 180 CE. (https://www.worldhistory.org/Antonine_Plague/ https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/what-rome-learned-deadly-antonine-plague-165-d-180974758/)

claim: Marcus Aurelius was succeeded by his own son Commodus, whose disastrous reign ended the era.
fact_check_evidence: Marcus Aurelius was succeeded by his biological son Commodus (180-192), whose reign is commonly held to end the Pax Romana and the era of the Five Good Emperors. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodus https://www.worldhistory.org/commodus/)

claim: By the time of Augustus, the city of Rome had perhaps around 1 million inhabitants, the largest city in the Western world.
tested_by: L61 question.ancient_rome.061.q1; L61 question.ancient_rome.061.q2; L66 question.ancient_rome.066.q3; L67 question.ancient_rome.067.q3; L70 question.ancient_rome.070.q1; L70 question.ancient_rome.070.q3
pre_check: Population estimates vary; confirm the page gives about 1 million.
fact_check_evidence: Common estimates put Augustan Rome near 1 million people, the largest city of its time, though some scholars argue for lower figures; the claim's 'perhaps around' hedges this adequately. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/BACD7DF32B0B77609CD6713B8AF88882/S0003598X00085859a.pdf/the-population-of-ancient-rome.pdf)

claim: Most people in Rome lived in insulae, crowded apartment blocks several stories high, usually without running water or private baths.
tested_by: L61 question.ancient_rome.061.q1; L61 question.ancient_rome.061.q2; L66 question.ancient_rome.066.q3; L67 question.ancient_rome.067.q3; L70 question.ancient_rome.070.q1; L70 question.ancient_rome.070.q3
fact_check_evidence: Most urban Romans lived in multi-story insulae; upper floors generally lacked running water, toilets and baths. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insula_(building) https://www.thecollector.com/insulae-roman-apartments/)

claim: In insulae the upper floors were the cheapest, and fire and collapse were constant dangers.
tested_by: L61 question.ancient_rome.061.q1; L61 question.ancient_rome.061.q2; L66 question.ancient_rome.066.q3; L67 question.ancient_rome.067.q3; L70 question.ancient_rome.070.q1; L70 question.ancient_rome.070.q3
fact_check_evidence: Upper floors of insulae had the lowest rents and were most dangerous; fires and building collapses were frequent hazards. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insula_(building) https://www.thecollector.com/insulae-roman-apartments/)

claim: Augustus set a height limit of about 20 meters for new buildings in Rome.
pre_check: Confirm the page gives the height limit.
fact_check_evidence: Augustus limited new buildings in Rome to 70 Roman feet (about 20.7 m) because of fire and collapse risks; Trajan later lowered it to 60 feet. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insula_(building) https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/curiosities/roman-skyscrapers/)

claim: Wealthy Romans lived in a domus, a private house built around an open hall called the atrium.
fact_check_evidence: The domus was the house of the Roman upper classes, centered on the atrium, a large hall open at the roof. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domus https://pompeiisites.org/en/pompeii-map/analysis/roman-housing/)

claim: The Forum was the center of Roman public life, with temples, law courts, markets and platforms for speeches.
fact_check_evidence: The Forum was the civic heart of Rome, with temples, basilicas used as law courts, markets and the Rostra speakers' platform. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Forum https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/roman-forum/)

claim: Augustus created the vigiles, a force of freedmen who fought fires and patrolled the streets at night.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions the vigiles.
fact_check_evidence: Augustus created the vigiles in 6 CE: seven cohorts recruited mainly from freedmen, who fought fires and served as a night watch. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigiles https://www.ostia-antica.org/dict/topics/caserma/intro.htm)

claim: Enslaved people made up a large share of the population of Roman Italy.
fact_check_evidence: Scheidel estimates up to about 1.5 million slaves in Roman Italy, roughly 15 to 25 percent of the population; older estimates are higher. (https://www.persee.fr/doc/topoi_1161-9473_1999_num_9_1_1808 https://gwern.net/doc/history/2005-scheidel.pdf)

claim: People were enslaved through war, piracy and trade, and children born to enslaved mothers were enslaved too.
fact_check_evidence: Roman slaves came from war captives, piracy and kidnapping, trade, and children born to enslaved mothers (vernae), who were slaves regardless of father. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_ancient_Rome https://www.worldhistory.org/article/629/slavery-in-the-roman-world/)

claim: Under Roman law an enslaved person was property, with no legal rights of their own.
fact_check_evidence: Roman law treated slaves as property lacking legal personhood; later imperial rules (Claudius, Antoninus Pius) limited owner abuse but did not grant slaves rights of their own. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_ancient_Rome https://www.unrv.com/articles/what-legal-rights-did-roman-slaves-have-if-any.php)

claim: Enslaved people did every kind of work, from mines and farms to households, and some served as teachers, doctors and secretaries.
fact_check_evidence: Enslaved people worked in mines, fields and households, and educated slaves served as teachers, doctors and secretaries. (https://www.unrv.com/articles/educated-slaves-in-ancient-rome.php https://www.unrv.com/articles/what-jobs-did-roman-slaves-do.php)

claim: Romans often freed enslaved people, a practice called manumission.
fact_check_evidence: Manumission was a common practice in Rome; owners freed slaves in considerable numbers, producing a large class of freedpeople. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Roman_freedmen https://www.pbs.org/empires/romans/empire/slaves_freemen.html)

claim: A person freed by a Roman citizen usually became a Roman citizen, and their children had full rights.
fact_check_evidence: Formally freed slaves of Roman citizens became citizens (with some limits, e.g. no office); their children born afterward were freeborn with full citizen rights. Informal manumission gave lesser status, hence 'usually'. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Roman_freedmen https://www.unrv.com/articles/children-of-freedmen-could-they-become-fully-roman.php)

claim: The poet Juvenal complained that the Roman people, who once handed out commands, now wanted only two things: bread and circuses.
fact_check_evidence: Juvenal, Satire 10: the people that once bestowed commands, consulships, legions and all else now longs for just two things, bread and circuses (panem et circenses). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bread_and_circuses https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Latin/JuvenalSatires10.php)

claim: Rome gave free grain to many citizens living in the city; under Augustus about 200,000 people received it.
pre_check: Confirm the page gives the number of recipients.
fact_check_evidence: Caesar cut the grain dole list to about 150,000; Augustus fixed the number of recipients at about 200,000. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cura_annonae https://www.unrv.com/articles/the-grain-dole-in-ancient-rome.php)

claim: Public games, ludi, began as religious festivals and grew into huge free entertainments.
fact_check_evidence: Ludi originated as votive religious offerings (e.g. Ludi Romani for Jupiter) and grew into large public spectacles on public holidays. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludi https://www.britannica.com/sports/ludi-publici)

claim: Emperors and politicians paid for games and food to win popularity and keep the city calm.
fact_check_evidence: Republican politicians and emperors used grain distributions and sponsored games to win popular support and reduce unrest (Juvenal's 'bread and circuses'). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bread_and_circuses https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cura_annonae)

claim: Emperors and politicians paid for games and food to win popularity and keep the city calm.
fact_check_evidence: Republican politicians and emperors used grain distributions and sponsored games to win popular support and reduce unrest (Juvenal's 'bread and circuses'). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bread_and_circuses https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cura_annonae)

claim: Gladiator fights probably began as funeral games to honor the dead, first recorded in Rome in 264 BCE.
fact_check_evidence: The first recorded gladiatorial combat in Rome was in 264 BC at the funeral of Decimus Junius Brutus Pera, as a munus for the dead. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gladiator https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum_Boarium)

claim: Most gladiators were enslaved people, prisoners of war or condemned criminals, but some free men volunteered.
fact_check_evidence: Gladiators were typically slaves, prisoners of war or condemned criminals; some free volunteers (auctorati) signed contracts to fight. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gladiator https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/gladiator/)

claim: Gladiators fought in types with set equipment, such as the net-and-trident retiarius against the helmeted secutor.
fact_check_evidence: Gladiator types had set equipment; the retiarius with net and trident was typically paired against the secutor with a smooth, egg-shaped helmet. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retiarius https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secutor)

claim: Gladiators were expensive to train, and many fights did not end in death: a beaten fighter could be spared.
pre_check: Confirm the page says defeated gladiators could be spared.
fact_check_evidence: Sources note gladiators were costly to train and keep, and a defeated fighter could be granted missio (spared); fights were often not to the death. (https://archive.archaeology.org/gladiators/glossary.html https://www.unrv.com/articles/did-gladiators-in-ancient-rome-always-fight-to-the-death.php)

claim: Roman writers mention a “turned thumb” deciding a gladiator’s fate, but its exact meaning is unknown.
pre_check: Confirm the page discusses the thumb gesture.
fact_check_evidence: Juvenal and Prudentius mention the 'turned thumb' (pollice verso), but whether the thumb pointed up, down or sideways, and what each meant, is unknown. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollice_verso https://time.com/4984728/thumbs-up-thumbs-down-history/)

claim: The Circus Maximus, Rome’s great racetrack, could hold about 150,000 spectators.
pre_check: Figures vary; confirm the page’s capacity.
fact_check_evidence: After Julius Caesar's enlargement the Circus Maximus held about 150,000 spectators; some later estimates (Pliny, Constantinian phase) run up to 250,000, so 'about 150,000' is a standard conservative figure. (https://www.digitalaugustanrome.org/records/circus-maximus/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circus_Maximus)

claim: Charioteers raced for four factions, the Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens, each with passionate fans.
fact_check_evidence: Roman chariot racing had four factions: Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens, with fiercely loyal fans (Domitian's Purples and Golds were short-lived). (http://vroma.org/vromans/bmcmanus/charioteer.html https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/blue-versus-green-rocking-the-byzantine-empire-113325928/)

claim: A standard race was seven laps around the central barrier, the spina.
fact_check_evidence: Races were generally seven laps around the spina, counted with egg and dolphin markers. (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/ancient-rome-circus-maximus-chariot-racing https://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_Romana/circusmaximus/circusmaximus.html)

claim: A standard race was seven laps around the central barrier, the spina.
fact_check_evidence: Races were generally seven laps around the spina, counted with egg and dolphin markers. (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/ancient-rome-circus-maximus-chariot-racing https://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_Romana/circusmaximus/circusmaximus.html)

claim: The most prestigious races used four-horse chariots, called quadrigae.
fact_check_evidence: Four-horse quadriga races were the most common and the crowd's favorite, the premier events of the Roman circus. (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_romana/circusmaximus/quadrigae.html https://www.history.com/articles/chariot-racing-ancient-rome)

claim: Successful charioteers could become rich and famous.
fact_check_evidence: Star charioteers such as Diocles (career winnings about 35.9 million sesterces) and Scorpus became wealthy celebrities. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Appuleius_Diocles https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/History/World_History/UnRoman_Romans_(McElduff)/03:_Entertainers/03.2:_Charioteers)

claim: In 532 CE fans of the Blues and Greens rioted together in Constantinople in the Nika revolt, nearly toppling the emperor Justinian.
fact_check_evidence: In January 532 the normally rival Blues and Greens united in the Nika riot, proclaimed a rival emperor and nearly drove Justinian to flee before Theodora persuaded him to stay. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nika_riots https://www.thecollector.com/what-was-the-nika-riot/)

claim: Large public baths, thermae, had hot, warm and cold rooms: the caldarium, tepidarium and frigidarium.
fact_check_evidence: Thermae had a caldarium (hot), tepidarium (warm) and frigidarium (cold) as core rooms. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/architecture/thermae https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tepidarium)

claim: Baths were heated by the hypocaust: hot air from furnaces flowed under raised floors and through the walls.
fact_check_evidence: Furnace (praefurnium) heat circulated under floors raised on pilae and rose through hollow box-tiles (tubuli) in the walls. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praefurnium https://www.unrv.com/articles/roman-hypocaust.php)

claim: The Baths of Caracalla, opened in the 3rd century CE, could serve about 1,600 bathers at a time.
tested_by: L66 question.ancient_rome.066.q2; L66 question.ancient_rome.066.q3; L70 question.ancient_rome.070.q5
pre_check: Confirm the page gives the capacity.
fact_check_evidence: Reference sources describe the Baths of Caracalla (opened c. 216 CE) as built for about 1,600 bathers at a time and up to around 8,000 a day. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baths_of_Caracalla https://www.unrv.com/rome/attractions/baths-of-caracalla.php)

claim: Instead of soap, bathers oiled their skin and scraped it clean with a curved metal tool, the strigil.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions oil and the strigil.
fact_check_evidence: Bathers applied olive oil and scraped off oil, sweat and dirt with a curved metal strigil; soap was not central to Roman bathing. (https://www.unrv.com/culture/strigil.php https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/lostempires/roman/tepidarium.html)

claim: Baths were social centers where Romans exercised, talked, did business and relaxed, and entry was cheap.
appears_in: L66 card.ancient_rome.066.c1; L66 card.ancient_rome.066.c3; L72 card.ancient_rome.072.c3
tested_by: L66 question.ancient_rome.066.q2; L66 question.ancient_rome.066.q3; L70 question.ancient_rome.070.q5
fact_check_evidence: Baths had palaestrae for exercise and were places to socialize and do business; entry was typically a quadrans, the smallest coin, and some were free. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Roman_bathing https://www.unrv.com/culture/roman-baths.php)

claim: Most Romans lived on grain, eaten as porridge or bread, with olive oil, wine, vegetables and beans.
fact_check_evidence: Grain as bread or puls supplied 70 to 80% of calories; the diet rested on cereals, vegetables, olive oil and wine, with legumes as key protein for the poor. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_in_ancient_Rome https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/roman-food-and-drink/)

claim: Garum, a fermented fish sauce, was one of the most popular seasonings in the Roman world.
fact_check_evidence: Garum, a fermented fish sauce, was one of the most important and widely used condiments in the Roman world. (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/what-is-garum-rome-fish-sauce https://theconversation.com/take-fish-salt-in-vats-leave-in-sun-for-months-why-ancient-romans-loved-fermented-fish-sauces-like-garum-260808)

claim: Garum was made in coastal factories, especially in Spain, and shipped around the empire in clay jars called amphorae.
fact_check_evidence: Major garum production centers were coastal salting factories in Hispania (e.g. Baelo Claudia); garum travelled across the empire in amphorae. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garum https://baeloclaudiaruins.com/guides/baelo-claudia-garum-roman-fish-sauce-industry/)

claim: Wealthy Romans held dinner parties in the triclinium, reclining on couches around a table.
fact_check_evidence: The triclinium was the formal dining room of wealthy Romans, with three couches around a table on which diners reclined. (https://www.unrv.com/culture/triclinium.php https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/triclinium)

claim: A Roman cookbook attributed to Apicius survives, with many recipes that use fish sauce.
fact_check_evidence: De re coquinaria, attributed to Apicius and likely compiled in the 4th century, is the only surviving Roman cookbook; most of its recipes call for fish sauce (liquamen/garum). (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/what-is-garum-rome-fish-sauce https://coquinaria.nl/en/roman-fish-sauce/)

claim: Romans had no tomatoes, potatoes or maize; these came from the Americas more than a thousand years later.
fact_check_evidence: Tomatoes, potatoes and maize are New World crops that reached Europe only after 1492, over a thousand years after the Western Roman Empire. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World_crops)

claim: Street counters called thermopolia sold hot food to city dwellers, many of whom had no kitchen at home.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions food counters.
fact_check_evidence: Thermopolia were street counters selling ready-to-eat hot food, used especially by insula dwellers without their own kitchens; about 158 are known at Pompeii. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermopolium https://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_Romana/wine/thermopolium.html)

claim: Latin was first spoken in Latium, the region around Rome.
fact_check_evidence: Latin originated as the language of the Latins of Latium, the region of central Italy around Rome. (https://www.britannica.com/place/Latium https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latins_(Italic_tribe))

claim: Everyday spoken Latin, often called Vulgar Latin, gradually developed into the Romance languages.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: Vulgar Latin, the everyday spoken language, is the chief source of the Romance languages. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Vulgar-Latin https://www.britannica.com/topic/Romance-languages/Latin-and-the-development-of-the-Romance-languages)

claim: Latin remained the language of the Western Church, law and scholarship for centuries after the Western Empire fell.
fact_check_evidence: After the Western Empire fell, Latin remained the language of the Church, scholarship, administration and law in Europe for centuries. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin https://www.britannica.com/topic/Latin-language)

claim: Romanian descends from the Latin spoken along the lower Danube, in Roman Dacia and the provinces south of the river. Scholars still debate exactly where it first took shape.
fact_check_evidence: Romanian descends from Danubian Vulgar Latin, but where it formed is debated: Daco-Roman continuity (north of the Danube) versus origins south of the Danube in Moesia and the Balkans with later migration north. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_the_Romanians https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanians)

claim: Latin spread through the western provinces with soldiers, settlers and officials, while Greek stayed the common language of the East.
fact_check_evidence: Latin became the dominant language of the western provinces (administration, army), while Koine Greek remained the lingua franca of the East. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_the_Roman_Empire https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_East_and_Latin_West)

claim: The Romance languages include Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian.
appears_in: L68 card.ancient_rome.068.c1; L68 card.ancient_rome.068.c3; L97 card.ancient_rome.097.c3
fact_check_evidence: The five major Romance languages are Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian and Romanian. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_languages)

claim: English is not a Romance language, but a large share of its vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it through French.
fact_check_evidence: English is Germanic, but roughly 29% of its vocabulary is from Latin and about as much from French; around 60% is Latin-derived directly or via Romance languages. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_influence_in_English https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign-language_influences_in_English)

claim: Roman women could not vote or hold political office.
fact_check_evidence: Freeborn Roman women were citizens but could not vote in assemblies or hold political office, though some exerted informal influence. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_ancient_Rome)

claim: Under early Roman law a woman needed a male guardian for legal matters, though the rule weakened over time.
fact_check_evidence: Tutela mulierum required a guardian for women's legal acts; it was weakened by Augustus' ius liberorum (9 CE) and eventually disappeared. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jus_trium_liberorum https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-roman-studies/article/end-of-tutela-mulierum/893480017AD050374B0ABDBD218050AB)

claim: Many Roman women owned property, ran businesses and inherited wealth.
fact_check_evidence: Freeborn Roman women could own and inherit property; evidence shows women owning brickworks and workshops, lending money and running businesses. (https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2726/roman-women-in-business/ https://www.unrv.com/culture/roman-women.php)

claim: Livia, the wife of Augustus, was one of the most influential people in Rome.
fact_check_evidence: Livia is described as the most powerful woman in the early Roman Empire and a key adviser to Augustus. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Livia-Drusilla https://www.worldhistory.org/Livia_Drusilla/)

claim: Roman daughters usually took a feminine form of the family name: Julius Caesar’s daughter was simply Julia.
pre_check: Confirm the naming practice on the page.
fact_check_evidence: Daughters took the feminine form of the father's nomen (Julius gives Julia); Caesar's daughter was known simply as Julia. (https://www.vroma.org/vromans/bmcmanus/roman_names.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_(daughter_of_Caesar))

claim: Roman girls from elite families were often married in their early to mid teens, usually to older men; most other girls probably married in their late teens.
pre_check: Confirm the page discusses marriage age.
fact_check_evidence: Elite girls often married at 12 to 15, but Saller and Shaw's study of epitaphs suggests most non-elite women first married in their late teens. Husbands were usually older. (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2006/2006.05.29/ https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2675/roman-girls-and-marriage-in-ancient-rome/)

claim: Life in Rome combined grand public spaces, such as baths, forums and arenas, with crowded and risky housing for most people.
fact_check_evidence: Most Romans lived in crowded insulae at risk of fire and collapse, in contrast with monumental baths, forums and temples. (https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/year-7/insulae/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insula_(building))

claim: Because homes were cramped, much of Roman life happened in public: in the streets, baths, forums and arenas.
fact_check_evidence: Small, kitchenless apartments pushed daily life into streets, taverns, public baths and forums. (https://www.worldhistory.org/article/637/roman-daily-life/ https://www.unrv.com/culture/streets-and-neighborhoods.php)

claim: Many Romans were clients of a wealthy patron, greeting him in the morning in return for help and protection.
pre_check: Confirm the page describes patrons and clients.
fact_check_evidence: Clients attended their patron's house at dawn for the salutatio, offering loyalty and support in return for protection, legal help and handouts (sportula). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage_in_ancient_Rome https://www.unrv.com/articles/patrons-and-clients-in-ancient-rome.php)

claim: At its height the Roman road network included more than 80,000 km of main roads.
pre_check: Confirm the page’s total length.
fact_check_evidence: Standard estimates give over 400,000 km of Roman roads, of which over 80,000 km were stone-paved main roads; a 2025 mapping study counts about 103,000 km of main roads, so 'more than 80,000 km' holds. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/roman-road-system https://theconversation.com/the-roman-empire-built-300-000-kilometres-of-roads-new-study-269186)

claim: Major Roman roads were built in layers: a foundation of large stones, then gravel or rubble, topped with paving stones.
fact_check_evidence: Major Roman roads used layers: statumen of large stones, rudus and nucleus of rubble/gravel and concrete, and a surface of paving slabs. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Roman_engineering https://www.britannica.com/technology/statumen)

claim: Roman roads ran as straight as the ground allowed and were cambered, curved slightly, so rainwater drained off.
fact_check_evidence: Roman roads took direct routes where terrain allowed but curved where needed; surfaces were cambered so rain ran off into side ditches. (https://www.romanobritain.org/12_innovations/inv_roads.php https://www.unrv.com/articles/how-roman-engineers-built-roads-that-still-exist.php)

claim: Milestones along Roman roads marked distances in Roman miles of 1,000 paces.
fact_check_evidence: The Roman mile (mille passuum) was 1,000 paces of 5 Roman feet; milestones (milliaria) stood along Roman roads marking distances in these miles. (http://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/e/roman/texts/secondary/smigra*/milliare.html https://www.unrv.com/articles/roman-milestones-and-roadside-infrastructure.php)

claim: Roman roads were built first for the army, letting legions march quickly, but they also carried trade, officials and the imperial post.
fact_check_evidence: Roman roads were built largely to move legions quickly, but also carried trade and the cursus publicus, the state courier system for officials and dispatches. (https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/learn/story-of-england/romans/networks/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cursus_publicus)

claim: Aqueducts carried water by gravity, along a gentle, steady downhill slope from springs in the hills.
tested_by: L72 question.ancient_rome.072.q1; L72 question.ancient_rome.072.q2; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q7
fact_check_evidence: Roman aqueducts moved water by gravity alone along a slight, steady downhill gradient; builders typically preferred springs as sources. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_aqueduct https://www.sciencenewstoday.org/roman-aqueducts-masterpieces-of-engineering)

claim: Most of an aqueduct’s length ran underground or at ground level; the famous arches carried it across valleys.
tested_by: L72 question.ancient_rome.072.q1; L72 question.ancient_rome.072.q2; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q7
fact_check_evidence: National Geographic: of about 315 miles of Rome's aqueducts, about 269 ran underground and only about 36 miles were on arches, used to cross valleys. (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/roman-aqueducts-engineering-innovation https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/roman-aqueducts/)

claim: Rome’s first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, was built in 312 BCE by Appius Claudius, who also began the Appian Way.
fact_check_evidence: The Aqua Appia, Rome's first aqueduct, was begun in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, who also built the Via Appia. (https://www.britannica.com/place/Aqua-Appia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_Appia)

claim: By the 3rd century CE, 11 aqueducts supplied the city of Rome.
fact_check_evidence: The Aqua Alexandrina, built under Alexander Severus in 226 CE, was the last of the eleven aqueducts of ancient Rome. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_Alexandrina https://www.turismoroma.it/en/places/alexandrian-aqueduct)

claim: The Pont du Gard in southern France is a surviving three-tier aqueduct bridge about 49 m high.
fact_check_evidence: The Pont du Gard near Nimes is a three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge 48.8 m high, the tallest Roman aqueduct bridge. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pont_du_Gard https://www.britannica.com/topic/Pont-du-Gard)

claim: Frontinus, Rome’s water commissioner around 97 CE, wrote a book about the city’s aqueducts.
fact_check_evidence: Frontinus was appointed curator aquarum by Nerva in AD 97 and wrote De aquaeductu, a two-book report on Rome's aqueducts. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curator_Aquarum https://penelope.uchicago.edu/encyclopaedia_romana/romanforum/quinaria.html)

claim: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash, called pozzolana, and chunks of rock or brick.
fact_check_evidence: Roman concrete combined a lime mortar with volcanic ash (pozzolana) and coarse aggregate (caementa) such as tuff, rock or brick fragments. (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.add1602)

claim: Pozzolana is named after Pozzuoli, near Naples, where the volcanic ash was dug.
fact_check_evidence: The name pozzolana derives from Pozzuoli (Roman Puteoli) on the Bay of Naples, a primary source of the volcanic ash used by the Romans. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pozzolana https://www.traditionalbuilding.com/opinions/15320-2)

claim: Concrete made with volcanic ash could set even underwater, which let Romans build harbors in the sea.
fact_check_evidence: Lime mixed with pozzolana (volcanic ash) produced hydraulic concrete that hardened underwater; Herod's harbor at Caesarea used large quantities imported from Puteoli. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_concrete https://web.uvic.ca/~jpoleson/ROMACONS/Caesarea2005.htm)

claim: Concrete let Romans build arches, vaults and domes on a scale never seen before.
fact_check_evidence: Roman concrete (opus caementicium) made arches, vaults and domes feasible at vast scale; the Pantheon dome is the classic example. (https://www.architecturecourses.org/learn/characteristics-roman-architecture https://www.theartnewbie.com/blog/rome/roman-concrete)

claim: Roman concrete walls were usually faced with brick or stone, so the concrete core was hidden.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions facing.
fact_check_evidence: Roman concrete walls were normally built with facings of small stones (opus reticulatum) or brick (opus testaceum) around a concrete core, which became the standard imperial method. (https://www.worldhistory.org/article/942/roman-walls/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opus_reticulatum)

claim: A 2023 study found that lumps of lime in Roman concrete could react with water to seal cracks, helping it last.
fact_check_evidence: A January 2023 MIT-led study in Science Advances found lime clasts in Roman concrete dissolve when cracks let in water and recrystallize to seal them. (https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106 https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/ancient-roman-concrete-has-self-healing-capabilities/)

claim: Pantheon means “of all the gods.”
fact_check_evidence: From Greek Pantheion, 'of, relating to, or common to all the gods' (pan 'all' + theion). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome https://www.etymonline.com/word/pantheon)

claim: The Pantheon’s dome, about 43 m across, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
fact_check_evidence: The Pantheon dome is about 43.3 m (142 ft) in diameter and is described as still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. (https://monolithicdome.com/pantheon https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_domes)

claim: An open hole at the top of the dome, the oculus, about 8 m wide, is the building’s only source of natural light.
pre_check: Confirm the oculus width.
fact_check_evidence: The Pantheon's oculus is about 8.2 m (27 ft) across and is described as the building's only source of natural light (apart from the entrance doors). (https://www.pantheonroma.com/en/2026/01/22/the-oculus-of-the-pantheon-architectural-marvel-of-ancient-rome/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oculus_(architecture))

claim: The height from the floor to the top of the Pantheon’s dome equals the dome’s diameter, so a complete sphere would fit inside.
fact_check_evidence: The Pantheon's interior diameter and height to the oculus are both about 43.3 m, so a full sphere would fit inside the rotunda. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome https://web.mit.edu/21h.405/www/Pantheon/Pantheon/Dome.html)

claim: The Pantheon’s dome gets thinner toward the top, and lighter stone was mixed into the concrete higher up.
pre_check: Confirm the page describes the graded aggregate.
fact_check_evidence: The Pantheon dome thins from about 6.4 m at the base to about 1.2 m at the oculus, and its aggregate grades from heavy travertine/basalt low down to light tuff and pumice near the top. (https://eandt.theiet.org/2022/03/15/pantheon-still-worlds-largest-unreinforced-concrete-dome)

claim: In 609 CE the Pantheon became a Christian church, which helped it survive intact.
fact_check_evidence: Pope Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon as the church of St Mary and the Martyrs on 13 May 609; sources credit the conversion with its survival. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02660c.htm https://www.history.com/articles/pantheon)

claim: Augustus split the provinces: peaceful ones had governors chosen by the Senate, while frontier provinces with armies were run by his own deputies.
fact_check_evidence: In 27 BC settled provinces stayed with Senate-chosen governors, while frontier provinces with legions were run by Augustus's legates. (https://www.unrv.com/articles/senatorial-vs-imperial-provinces.php https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legate_(ancient_Rome))

claim: Provinces paid taxes on land and on people, and a census counted them for taxation.
fact_check_evidence: Provincial tribute consisted mainly of a land tax (tributum soli) and a poll tax (tributum capitis), assessed through periodic provincial censuses. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tributum_capitis https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_ancient_Rome)

claim: In the Republic, tax collection was often contracted out to private companies of publicani, who were notorious for abuses.
fact_check_evidence: Republican tax collection was farmed out to companies of publicani (societates publicanorum), widely accused of greed and abuses in the provinces. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publicani https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Societates_publicanorum)

claim: Rome ran its provinces with few officials, relying on local elites to govern their own cities and collect taxes.
appears_in: L75 card.ancient_rome.075.c1; L75 card.ancient_rome.075.c3; L80 card.ancient_rome.080.c2
fact_check_evidence: Rome governed with strikingly few officials, leaving administration and tax collection largely to city councils and local elites. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_government_in_ancient_Rome https://www.unrv.com/articles/how-rome-collected-taxes-from-the-provinces.php)

claim: Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect who governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Pilate succeeded Valerius Gratus as prefect of Judaea in 26 CE and held the post about ten years, to 36 CE. (https://www.livius.org/articles/person/pontius-pilate/ https://www.britannica.com/summary/Pontius-Pilate)

claim: Roman citizens had legal privileges, such as the right to appeal to Rome and protection from certain punishments.
fact_check_evidence: Citizens had provocatio (right of appeal, later to the emperor) and the Valerian and Porcian laws protected them from flogging and crucifixion. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valerian_and_Porcian_laws)

claim: During the Social War of 91–88 BCE, Rome granted citizenship to its Italian allies, first to those who stayed loyal and then to the rest, which helped end the revolt.
tested_by: L76 question.ancient_rome.076.q2; L76 question.ancient_rome.076.q3; L79 question.ancient_rome.079.q3; L80 question.ancient_rome.080.q5
fact_check_evidence: Citizenship came during the war, not after it: the Lex Julia (90 BCE) and Lex Plautia Papiria (89 BCE) granted it to loyal and then surrendering allies, which helped end the revolt. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Plautia_Papiria https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Julia)

claim: Citizenship spread through the provinces by grants to towns, to individuals and to soldiers.
tested_by: L76 question.ancient_rome.076.q2; L76 question.ancient_rome.076.q3; L79 question.ancient_rome.079.q3; L80 question.ancient_rome.080.q5
fact_check_evidence: Enfranchisement came via grants to individuals, block grants to whole communities, and citizenship for auxiliary veterans on discharge (plus manumission). (https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/bitstream/handle/10023/12646/Lavan_2016_PandP_SpreadRomanCitizenship_RevisedAAM.pdf https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_military_diploma)

claim: Non-citizen soldiers, the auxiliaries, received Roman citizenship after about 25 years of service.
tested_by: L76 question.ancient_rome.076.q2; L76 question.ancient_rome.076.q3; L79 question.ancient_rome.079.q3; L80 question.ancient_rome.080.q5
pre_check: Confirm the page gives the service length.
fact_check_evidence: Livius and the Wikipedia article on military diplomas state auxiliaries (non-citizen peregrini) received citizenship on discharge after 25 years of service, recorded on a bronze diploma. (https://www.livius.org/articles/legion/auxiliaries/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_military_diploma)

claim: In 212 CE the emperor Caracalla granted citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.
appears_in: L76 card.ancient_rome.076.c1; L76 card.ancient_rome.076.c4; L80 card.ancient_rome.080.c2
tested_by: L76 question.ancient_rome.076.q1; L80 question.ancient_rome.080.q2; L80 question.ancient_rome.080.q5; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q8
fact_check_evidence: The Constitutio Antoniniana of AD 212 granted Roman citizenship to free inhabitants of the empire, with limited exceptions such as the dediticii. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutio_Antoniniana https://www.unesco.org/en/memory-world/constitutio-antoniniana)

claim: According to the Book of Acts, Paul of Tarsus, a Roman citizen, used his right to appeal to the emperor.
fact_check_evidence: Acts 25:11 has Paul, a Roman citizen, declare 'I appeal to Caesar' before Festus, and he is sent to Rome. (https://www.bibleref.com/Acts/25/Acts-25-11.html https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/)

claim: Roman legal experts, the jurists, wrote opinions that developed and explained the law.
fact_check_evidence: Jurists' responsa (opinions) were highly influential, recognized as a source of law, and were excerpted into Justinian's Digest. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsa https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/law/law-divisions-and-codes/roman-law)

claim: Roman jurists held that the burden of proof rests on the person who makes a claim, not on the one who denies it.
pre_check: The maxim is in the Digest; confirm a source states it.
fact_check_evidence: Digest 22.3.2 (Paul): 'Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat', proof lies on the one who asserts, not the one who denies. (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/justinian/digest22.shtml https://www.trans-lex.org/800200/)

claim: Many legal terms in English are Latin, such as alibi, meaning “elsewhere.”
pre_check: Confirm or cite a dictionary.
fact_check_evidence: Etymonline and Latin dictionaries give Latin alibi as an adverb meaning 'elsewhere' (locative of alius); it entered English law c. 1743 as a plea of having been elsewhere. (https://www.etymonline.com/word/alibi https://www.latin-is-simple.com/en/vocabulary/phrase/112/)

claim: In the 6th century CE the emperor Justinian had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “body of civil law.”
tested_by: L77 question.ancient_rome.077.q1; L80 question.ancient_rome.080.q5; L95 question.ancient_rome.095.q3
fact_check_evidence: The Corpus Juris Civilis (Body of Civil Law) was compiled 529 to 534 by order of Justinian I. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Juris_Civilis https://www.worldhistory.org/Corpus_Juris_Civilis/)

claim: Justinian’s code shaped the civil law systems used across continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries.
appears_in: L77 card.ancient_rome.077.c1; L77 card.ancient_rome.077.c3; L96 card.ancient_rome.096.c3
tested_by: L77 question.ancient_rome.077.q1; L80 question.ancient_rome.080.q5; L95 question.ancient_rome.095.q3
fact_check_evidence: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis, revived from the 11th century, became the foundation of civil law systems in continental Europe, Latin America and parts of Africa. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Juris_Civilis https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_law)

claim: The denarius, a silver coin, was the standard Roman coin for centuries.
fact_check_evidence: The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin from about 211 BCE to the mid 3rd century CE, when the antoninianus replaced it. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denarius https://www.unrv.com/economy/coins/denarius.php)

claim: Roman coins carried the emperor’s portrait and short messages, spreading his image across the empire.
fact_check_evidence: Imperial coins usually bore the ruler's portrait on the obverse and slogans or messages on the reverse, circulating his image across the empire. (https://www.cultureoncall.com/the-propaganda-of-roman-coins/ https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/article/propaganda-on-roman-coins/)

claim: Wine, olive oil and fish sauce moved around the Mediterranean in amphorae, clay jars made for shipping.
fact_check_evidence: Amphorae were ceramic transport jars used in vast numbers, mostly for wine, olive oil and garum (fish sauce), shipped across the Mediterranean. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphora https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_commerce)

claim: Monte Testaccio in Rome is an artificial hill made of fragments of millions of broken olive oil amphorae.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions Monte Testaccio.
fact_check_evidence: Monte Testaccio is a 35 m artificial mound made mainly of fragments of an estimated 53 million olive oil amphorae, mostly from Baetica, dumped c. 1st-3rd centuries CE. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Testaccio https://www.oliveoiltimes.com/world/monte-testaccio-remnants-ancient-trade/46185)

claim: Roman traders sailed to India, and Chinese silk reached Rome through many middlemen along the Silk Road.
fact_check_evidence: Roman ships used monsoon winds to trade directly with India; Chinese silk reached Rome via Central Asian, Parthian, Indian and other intermediaries. (https://www.thecollector.com/roman-trade-with-india-and-china-explained/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Roman_trade_relations)

claim: Over time emperors reduced the silver in the denarius, and by the 3rd century CE it held very little.
tested_by: L78 question.ancient_rome.078.q1; L78 question.ancient_rome.078.q2; L81 question.ancient_rome.081.q2
fact_check_evidence: Debasement began under Nero (64 CE); Caracalla cut fineness to about 50%, and by Gallienus (c. 260) silver content was around 5% or less, with about 2% by later 3rd century. (https://www.thecollector.com/inflation-third-century-crisis/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denarius)

claim: The fortified frontier of the Roman Empire was called the limes.
fact_check_evidence: Limes, originally a boundary path, came to denote the fortified frontier systems of the Roman Empire. (https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/430 https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/limes/)

claim: Much of the frontier was held by auxiliaries, non-citizen soldiers recruited from the provinces.
fact_check_evidence: Auxilia were non-citizen soldiers recruited from the provinces; most units garrisoned frontier forts and by the 2nd century they made up over half of the regular army. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxilia https://www.unrv.com/military/auxiliaries.php)

claim: Roman forts followed a standard plan: a rectangle with rounded corners, four gates and a headquarters building at the center.
pre_check: Confirm the page describes the fort plan.
fact_check_evidence: Imperial-era forts were typically playing-card shaped (rectangles with rounded corners), with four gates and the principia (headquarters) at the centre. (https://romansinscotland.com/roman-fort-layout/ https://acoup.blog/2021/11/12/collections-fortification-part-ii-roman-playing-cards/)

claim: Civilian settlements grew up beside frontier forts, with traders, craftsmen and soldiers’ families.
fact_check_evidence: Civilian settlements (vici) grew beside forts, housing traders, craftsmen, innkeepers and soldiers' families. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicus https://www.northeastmuseums.org.uk/segedunum/learning/the-civilian-settlement-around-the-fort)

claim: At Vindolanda, a fort near Hadrian’s Wall, archaeologists found more than a thousand wooden writing tablets, including a birthday invitation from one commander’s wife to another.
appears_in: L79 card.ancient_rome.079.c1; L79 card.ancient_rome.079.c4; L98 card.ancient_rome.098.c4
fact_check_evidence: More than 1,700 tablets have been found at Vindolanda, so 'hundreds' understates it. Tablet 291 is Claudia Severa's birthday invitation to Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of the Vindolanda commander. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vindolanda_tablets https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/galleries/roman-britain/vindolanda-tablets https://romaninscriptionsofbritain.org/inscriptions/TabVindol291)

claim: Rome held its empire together with roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade, not by force alone.
fact_check_evidence: Sources describe roads, citizenship grants, Roman law, trade and army service as integrating the provinces, beyond military force. (https://www.unrv.com/articles/how-roman-roads-connected-the-provinces.php https://www.worldhistory.org/article/859/roman-citizenship/)

claim: Historians call the spread of Roman language, culture and ways of life in the provinces Romanization; towns across the West built forums, baths and amphitheaters on the Roman model.
