fact_check_evidence: Romanization is the standard term for adoption of Latin, Roman law and Roman-style buildings (forums, baths, amphitheaters) in provincial towns. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_amphitheatre https://www.unrv.com/articles/romanization-in-gaul-how-deep-did-it-go.php)

claim: From 235 to 284 CE, the Crisis of the Third Century, the empire suffered civil wars, invasions, plague and economic trouble.
fact_check_evidence: The Crisis of the Third Century (235 to 284) combined civil war, invasions, plague, currency debasement and economic depression. (https://www.worldhistory.org/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century)

claim: In about 50 years of crisis there were more than 20 emperors, most of whom were killed in office.
pre_check: Counts vary; confirm the page’s figure.
fact_check_evidence: For 235 to 284 CE sources count roughly 20 to 26 emperors or claimants, the large majority assassinated or killed; counts vary by criteria but 'more than 20, most killed' fits. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century https://www.worldhistory.org/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century/)

claim: In 260 CE the emperor Valerian was captured by the Persian king Shapur I, the first Roman emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy.
fact_check_evidence: Sources call Valerian (captured by Shapur I in 260) the FIRST Roman emperor taken prisoner. He was not the only one: Byzantine (Eastern Roman) emperor Romanos IV Diogenes was captured by the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan at Manzikert in 1071. (https://www.worldhistory.org/valerian/ https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Manzikert https://www.worldhistory.org/Romanos_IV_Diogenes/)

claim: For a time the empire split into three: a breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, Rome in the middle, and Palmyra under Queen Zenobia in the east.
fact_check_evidence: During the Crisis of the Third Century the empire split into the Gallic Empire, the Italian-centered Roman Empire and the Palmyrene Empire under Zenobia. (https://www.worldatlas.com/ancient-world/what-was-the-crisis-of-the-third-century.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century)

claim: The emperor Aurelian reunited the empire in the 270s and built new walls around Rome.
fact_check_evidence: Aurelian (270 to 275) reconquered the Palmyrene Empire (273) and the Gallic Empire (274), reuniting the empire; work on the Aurelian Walls began in 271. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelian https://allthatsinteresting.com/aurelian)

claim: Diocletian became emperor in 284 CE and ended the half century of crisis.
tested_by: L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q1; L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q2; L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q3; L90 question.ancient_rome.090.q1
fact_check_evidence: Sources say Diocletian seized power in 284 and is credited with decisively ending the Crisis of the Third Century (235 to 284) and restoring effective government. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century https://www.worldhistory.org/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century/)

claim: Diocletian created the Tetrarchy, “rule of four”: two senior emperors, called Augusti, and two junior ones, called Caesars.
tested_by: L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q1; L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q2; L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q3; L90 question.ancient_rome.090.q1
fact_check_evidence: The Tetrarchy ('rule of four', from 293) had two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrarchy https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome/Diocletian)

claim: The Tetrarchy was meant to put an emperor near every threatened frontier and give the empire a planned succession.
tested_by: L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q1; L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q2; L82 question.ancient_rome.082.q3; L90 question.ancient_rome.090.q1
fact_check_evidence: Diocletian's Tetrarchy placed emperors near major frontier zones (Nicomedia, Milan, Thessalonica, Trier) and set out a planned succession of Caesars to Augusti. (https://www.unrv.com/articles/the-tetrarchy-explained-four-emperors-one-empire.php https://www.britannica.com/biography/Diocletian/Reorganization-of-the-empire)

claim: Diocletian split the provinces into smaller units and separated civil from military command.
fact_check_evidence: Diocletian roughly doubled the provinces (about 50 to about 100) and separated civil governors from military command. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Diocletian/Domestic-reforms https://www.unrv.com/government/reforms-of-civil-military-command.php)

claim: In 301 CE Diocletian’s Edict on Maximum Prices tried, and failed, to stop inflation by fixing prices.
fact_check_evidence: Diocletian's 301 CE edict set maximum prices and wages to curb inflation; it failed, causing hoarding and black markets. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices https://www.econlib.org/diocletian-the-roman-empire-and-forever-failing-price-controls/)

claim: In 305 CE Diocletian retired, the first Roman emperor to step down voluntarily, to his palace at Split in modern Croatia.
fact_check_evidence: Diocletian left office on 1 May 305, the first Roman emperor to abdicate voluntarily, and retired to his palace at Spalatum, the core of modern Split, Croatia. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletian https://www.historytoday.com/archive/abdication-emperor-diocletian)

claim: Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish teacher executed by crucifixion in Judaea under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate.
fact_check_evidence: Jesus's execution under Pilate, prefect of Judaea, is among the most secure facts of early Christianity, attested by the Gospels and Tacitus. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontius_Pilate https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/who-was-the-real-pontius-pilate-christianity-trial-of-jesus)

claim: Paul of Tarsus spread Christianity to non-Jews in cities around the eastern Mediterranean.
fact_check_evidence: Between about 47 and 56 AD Paul travelled the eastern Mediterranean founding churches and spreading his faith to gentiles. (https://omniatlas.com/maps/eastern-mediterranean/480125/ https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2515/the-journeys-of-paul-the-apostle/)

claim: Christianity spread mainly in cities, helped by Roman roads, peace and the common Greek language of the East.
fact_check_evidence: Sources cite Roman roads, Pax Romana stability and Koine Greek as a common language as key factors; early churches were in cities such as Antioch, Ephesus, Corinth and Rome. (https://www.history.com/articles/5-ways-christianity-spread-through-ancient-rome https://www.gotquestions.org/Pax-Romana.html)

claim: Christians worshiped one God and refused to sacrifice to the Roman gods or to the emperor.
fact_check_evidence: Early Christians believed in one God and refused to sacrifice to Roman gods or the emperor, which led to persecution. (https://uscatholic.org/articles/202207/why-did-the-romans-persecute-christians/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decian_persecution)

claim: Christian communities were led by bishops and cared for their poor, widows and sick.
fact_check_evidence: Early churches were led by bishops and organized care for widows, the poor and sick; in 251 the Roman church under Bishop Cornelius supported over 1,500 widows and needy people. (https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/new-era-in-roman-healthcare https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/healing-the-city)

claim: For most of the first two centuries, persecution of Christians was local and sporadic, not constant.
fact_check_evidence: Until Decius (249 to 251) persecution of Christians was local and sporadic; Decius's edict was the first empire-wide one. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/religion-and-philosophy/outbreak-decian-persecution https://academic.oup.com/past/article/261/1/3/6982747)

claim: Pliny the Younger, as a governor, asked Trajan how to treat Christians; Trajan replied that they should not be hunted out, but punished if accused and they refused to recant.
fact_check_evidence: Trajan replied to Pliny (governor of Bithynia-Pontus) that Christians should not be sought out, but if accused and convicted should be punished unless they recanted by worshipping the gods. (https://faculty.georgetown.edu/jod/texts/pliny.html http://www.earlychristianwritings.com/text/pliny2.html)

claim: In 250 CE the emperor Decius ordered everyone in the empire to sacrifice to the gods, the first empire-wide persecution.
tested_by: L84 question.ancient_rome.084.q1; L84 question.ancient_rome.084.q3; L85 question.ancient_rome.085.q3
fact_check_evidence: Decius's edict (c. Jan 250) ordered all inhabitants to sacrifice before magistrates with certificates; Britannica calls it the first organized persecution of Christians throughout the empire; earlier persecutions were local. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Decius https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decian_persecution)

claim: The Great Persecution under Diocletian, from 303 CE, was the harshest the Christians faced.
appears_in: L84 card.ancient_rome.084.c3; L85 card.ancient_rome.085.c1; L88 card.ancient_rome.088.c1
tested_by: L84 question.ancient_rome.084.q1; L84 question.ancient_rome.084.q3; L85 question.ancient_rome.085.q3
fact_check_evidence: The Diocletianic or Great Persecution, begun with edicts in 303, is described as the last and most severe persecution of Christians in the empire. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletianic_Persecution https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/religion-and-philosophy/diocletianic-persecution/)

claim: Refusing to sacrifice to the gods and the emperor looked like disloyalty, and Romans feared it would break the peace with the gods.
fact_check_evidence: Refusing sacrifice to the gods and the emperor was seen as subversive and as endangering the pax deorum (peace with the gods). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decian_persecution https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/curiosities/pax-deorum/)

claim: Christians who died for their faith were honored as martyrs, from a Greek word meaning “witness.”
fact_check_evidence: 'Martyr' comes from Greek martys, literally 'witness', which took on the sense of one who dies for the faith. (https://www.etymonline.com/word/martyr)

claim: In 312 CE Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica and History Today: Constantine defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge on the Tiber near Rome, 28 October 312 CE; Maxentius drowned. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-the-Milvian-Bridge https://www.historytoday.com/archive/battle-milvian-bridge)

claim: Christian writers said Constantine saw a sign before the battle and had his soldiers fight under a Christian symbol.
fact_check_evidence: Lactantius and Eusebius report a dream or vision before the Milvian Bridge (312) and that soldiers bore the Chi-Rho on shields or the labarum; framed correctly as their claim. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Milvian_Bridge https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-the-Milvian-Bridge)

claim: In 313 CE, the Edict of Milan granted religious tolerance to Christians throughout the empire.
tested_by: L85 question.ancient_rome.085.q1; L85 question.ancient_rome.085.q2; L85 question.ancient_rome.085.q3; L87 question.ancient_rome.087.q3; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q10
fact_check_evidence: In 313 Constantine and Licinius agreed at Milan to grant Christians (and all religions) freedom of worship and return confiscated property. (https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/edict-of-milan https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/edict-milan/)

claim: By 324 CE Constantine had defeated his last rival and ruled the whole empire alone.
fact_check_evidence: Constantine defeated Licinius at Chrysopolis on 18 September 324 and became sole ruler of the empire. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chrysopolis https://www.worldhistory.org/Constantine_I/)

claim: In 325 CE Constantine called the Council of Nicaea, a meeting of bishops that agreed a common statement of Christian belief.
tested_by: L85 question.ancient_rome.085.q1; L85 question.ancient_rome.085.q2; L85 question.ancient_rome.085.q3; L87 question.ancient_rome.087.q3; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q10
fact_check_evidence: Constantine convened about 300 bishops at Nicaea in 325 CE; they produced the Nicene Creed, a shared statement of belief. (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/christianity-nicene-creed-first-council-of-nicaea https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/council-nicaea/)

claim: Constantine was baptized only on his deathbed, in 337 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Constantine was baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia in May 337, days before he died on 22 May 337, as recorded by Eusebius of Caesarea. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eusebius_of_Nicomedia https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05623b.htm)

claim: Constantinople stood on the Bosporus, the strait between Europe and Asia, controlling the route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
appears_in: L86 card.ancient_rome.086.c1; L86 card.ancient_rome.086.c2; L86 card.ancient_rome.086.c4
fact_check_evidence: The Bosporus separates Europe and Asia and, with the Sea of Marmara and Dardanelles, is the only passage between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean; Constantinople controlled it. (https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Bosporus https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosporus)

claim: The new capital was closer than Rome to the threatened Danube and eastern frontiers.
fact_check_evidence: Sources note Rome was far from the frontiers, while Constantinople was a strong base for guarding the Danube and reasonably close to the eastern frontier. (https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Constantinople https://www.unrv.com/articles/why-did-rome-move-its-capital-to-constantinople.php)

claim: Constantinople was built as a new Rome, with its own senate, forums and a great hippodrome for chariot racing.
fact_check_evidence: Constantine proclaimed the city a New Rome, with a forum, a senate house and an enlarged hippodrome modelled on the Circus Maximus. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum_of_Constantine https://penelope.uchicago.edu/encyclopaedia_romana/circusmaximus/hippodrome.html)

claim: Constantinople is today Istanbul, in Turkey.
fact_check_evidence: Constantinople is modern Istanbul, Turkey; the name was made official in 1930. (https://www.livescience.com/istanbul-not-constantinople https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Istanbul)

claim: Constantine dedicated his new capital, Constantinople, on the site of the Greek city of Byzantium in 330 CE.
appears_in: L86 card.ancient_rome.086.c2; L90 card.ancient_rome.090.c2; L95 card.ancient_rome.095.c4; L95 card.ancient_rome.095.c2
fact_check_evidence: On 11 May 330 Constantine dedicated Byzantium, a Greek colony, as his new capital, Constantinople (New Rome). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople https://greekcitytimes.com/2021/05/12/may-11-330-byzantium/)

claim: Julian, Constantine’s nephew, became sole emperor in 361 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Julian, son of Constantine's half-brother Julius Constantius, became sole emperor when Constantius II died on 3 November 361. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08558b.htm https://www.britannica.com/summary/Julian-Roman-emperor)

claim: Julian rejected Christianity and tried to restore worship of the traditional gods.
fact_check_evidence: Julian renounced Christianity and reopened temples, restored temple lands and priesthoods to revive traditional worship. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_of_paganism_from_Julian_until_Valens https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_(emperor))

claim: Christians called him Julian the Apostate: an apostate is someone who abandons their faith.
fact_check_evidence: Julian is called 'the Apostate' in Christian tradition because he rejected his Christian upbringing; an apostate is one who renounces a faith. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_(emperor) https://orthodoxwiki.org/Julian_the_Apostate)

claim: Julian was the last Roman emperor to follow the traditional gods.
fact_check_evidence: Julian (ruled 361-363) is widely described as the last pagan Roman emperor, who tried to restore traditional worship. (https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Julian_the_Apostate https://ehrmanblog.org/who-was-the-last-non-christian-emperor-of-rome/)

claim: Julian banned Christians from teaching classical literature.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions the teaching edict.
fact_check_evidence: Julian's school edict of 17 June 362 barred Christian teachers from teaching the pagan classics (grammar, rhetoric) unless they acknowledged the gods. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_(emperor) https://blogs.nottingham.ac.uk/mintimperials/2015/06/17/on-this-day-in-ad362-julian-banned-christians-from-teaching-using-pagan-literature/)

claim: Julian was killed on campaign against Persia in 363 CE, and his religious program died with him.
fact_check_evidence: Julian was mortally wounded on 26 June 363 during his Persian campaign; his attempted pagan restoration did not survive him. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ctesiphon_(363) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_of_paganism_from_Julian_until_Valens)

claim: In 380 CE, under Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity became the official religion of the empire.
tested_by: L88 question.ancient_rome.088.q1; L88 question.ancient_rome.088.q3; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q10
fact_check_evidence: The Edict of Thessalonica (27 Feb 380), issued by Theodosius I with Gratian and Valentinian II, made Nicene Christianity the state church of the empire. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Thessalonica https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/religion-and-philosophy/theodosiuss-edicts-promote-christian-orthodoxy)

claim: In the 390s Theodosius banned sacrifices and closed temples.
tested_by: L88 question.ancient_rome.088.q1; L88 question.ancient_rome.088.q3; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q10
fact_check_evidence: Theodosian decrees of 391-392 banned sacrifice and access to temples (Rome 391, Alexandria 392); Britannica describes temples closed under Theodosius. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Theodosius-I/The-middle-years https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_pagans_under_Theodosius_I)

claim: The ancient Olympic Games are traditionally said to have ended in 393 CE under Theodosius.
fact_check_evidence: 393 CE under Theodosius is the widely cited traditional end date; some historians question it, but the claim is framed as tradition. (https://www.olympics.com/ioc/ioc-overview/ioc-history/ancient-olympics/the-end-of-the-ancient-games https://theconversation.com/mythbusting-ancient-rome-did-christians-ban-the-ancient-olympics-92023)

claim: In the 390s the sacred fire of Vesta was put out and the Vestal Virgins were disbanded.
tested_by: L88 question.ancient_rome.088.q1; L88 question.ancient_rome.088.q3; L100 question.ancient_rome.100.q10
pre_check: Confirm the page gives the date.
fact_check_evidence: Under Theodosius I's anti-pagan measures the sacred fire of Vesta was extinguished and the Vestal college disbanded, usually dated to 394 CE (some say 391). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_fire_of_Vesta https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestal_Virgin)

claim: Bishop Ambrose of Milan made Theodosius do public penance for a massacre at Thessalonica, showing the church’s new power.
fact_check_evidence: After the massacre at Thessalonica (c. 390), Ambrose barred Theodosius from communion until he did public penance, a landmark in church-state relations. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_Thessalonica)

claim: Theodosius was the last emperor to rule both halves of the empire; after his death in 395 CE it was divided between his two sons.
fact_check_evidence: Theodosius I was the last emperor to rule both eastern and western halves (392 to 395); on his death in 395 the empire passed to his sons Arcadius (East) and Honorius (West). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosian_dynasty https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcadius)

claim: In 376 CE Goths fleeing the Huns were allowed to cross the Danube into the empire.
fact_check_evidence: In 376 Goths under Fritigern, fleeing the Huns, asked Valens for refuge and were allowed to cross the Danube. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_War_(376%E2%80%93382) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritigern)

claim: The Huns, nomadic horsemen from the Eurasian steppes, were pushing west in the 370s, driving other peoples before them.
fact_check_evidence: The Huns, steppe nomads, reached the Volga by about 370 and subdued the Alans and Goths (370 to 375), pushing peoples toward the Roman frontier. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/anthropology-and-archaeology/people/huns)

claim: Mistreated and exploited by Roman officials, the Goths rebelled.
fact_check_evidence: In 376 officials Lupicinus and Maximus extorted and starved the settled Goths, who then revolted, leading to Adrianople (378). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_War_(376%E2%80%93382) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lupicinus_(comes_per_Thracias))

claim: At Adrianople in 378 CE the Goths destroyed a Roman army, and the emperor Valens was killed.
fact_check_evidence: On 9 August 378 near Adrianople the Goths under Fritigern destroyed a Roman army; Emperor Valens died on the battlefield. (https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Adrianople-378 https://www.worldhistory.org/Battle_of_Adrianople/)

claim: Gothic cavalry arriving during the battle played a decisive part in the Roman defeat.
fact_check_evidence: At Adrianople (378 CE) Gothic cavalry returning during the battle struck the Roman army, a decisive factor in the defeat and death of Valens. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Adrianople https://www.thecollector.com/what-happened-at-the-battle-of-adrianople-378-ad/)

claim: Afterwards, Gothic groups settled inside the empire as allies under their own leaders, a new and risky arrangement.
fact_check_evidence: The 382 treaty settled Goths inside the empire as semi-autonomous foederati not under direct Roman administration, the first such arrangement; they fought under their own commanders. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_I https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaric_I)

claim: By 395 CE the empire was Christian, divided into East and West, and defended partly by Germanic allies under their own leaders.
fact_check_evidence: On Theodosius' death in 395 the empire was split East and West; Christianity had been made the state religion under him; Goths settled as foederati fought for Rome under their own leaders. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosian_dynasty https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Thessalonica https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_War_(376%E2%80%93382))

claim: Later emperors ruled more openly as absolute monarchs, surrounded by elaborate court ceremony; historians sometimes call this the Dominate, from dominus, “lord.”
pre_check: Confirm the page uses the term Dominate.
fact_check_evidence: The term Dominate (from dominus, 'lord/master') describes the later empire from Diocletian on, marked by open autocracy and elaborate court ceremony such as prostration before the emperor. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominate https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/dominate-rome)

claim: By 410 CE the western emperor Honorius lived at Ravenna, a city protected by marshes, not in Rome.
fact_check_evidence: Honorius moved the western court to marsh-protected Ravenna in 402 and was there when Alaric sacked Rome in 410. (https://www.historyhit.com/what-happened-to-roman-emperors-after-rome-was-sacked-in-410/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410))

claim: Stilicho, the western empire’s leading general, had held the Visigoth leader Alaric off, but he was executed in 408 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Stilicho, the West's leading general who had repeatedly checked Alaric, was arrested at Ravenna and beheaded on 22 August 408. (https://www.worldhistory.org/Stilicho/ https://www.executedtoday.com/2008/08/22/408-stilicho-alaric-honorius-visigoths/)

claim: In 410 CE the Visigoths under Alaric sacked Rome, the first time the city had fallen to a foreign enemy in about 800 years.
fact_check_evidence: Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in August 410, the first time in close to 800 years the city fell to a foreign enemy (previous: the Gallic sack c. 390/387 BC). (https://www.britannica.com/event/Sack-of-Rome-410 https://colorado.pressbooks.pub/warandsocietysourcebook/chapter/accounts-of-the-sack-of-rome/)

claim: Alaric’s troops plundered Rome for three days.
fact_check_evidence: Alaric's Goths entered Rome on 24 August 410 and plundered it for three days. (https://www.britannica.com/event/Sack-of-Rome-410 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410))

claim: The scholar Jerome wrote that the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken.
pre_check: Confirm the page quotes Jerome on the sack.
fact_check_evidence: Writing from Bethlehem about Alaric's sack of Rome in 410, Jerome said the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken (Letter 127). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410) https://colorado.pressbooks.pub/warandsocietysourcebook/chapter/accounts-of-the-sack-of-rome/)

claim: Augustine of Hippo wrote The City of God partly to answer pagans who blamed the sack on the abandonment of the old gods.
fact_check_evidence: Augustine wrote The City of God (c. 413-426) in response to pagan claims that the 410 sack of Rome resulted from abandoning the traditional gods. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-City-of-God https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_City_of_God)

claim: Attila ruled the Huns from 434 to 453 CE, at first jointly with his brother Bleda.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: Attila was king of the Huns from 434 to 453, ruling jointly with his elder brother Bleda until about 445, when he murdered him. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Attila-king-of-the-Huns https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleda)

claim: Attila raided the Eastern Empire and forced it to pay him large amounts of gold.
fact_check_evidence: After invading the Eastern Empire in the 440s, Attila forced Theodosius II to pay 6,000 pounds of gold in arrears and a tripled annual tribute of 2,100 pounds. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Attila-king-of-the-Huns https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Attila_the_Hun)

claim: In 451 CE a Roman and Visigothic army under the general Aetius stopped Attila’s invasion of Gaul at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains.
fact_check_evidence: In 451 a coalition led by Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric (with Franks, Alans and others) fought Attila on the Catalaunian Plains, ending his invasion of Gaul. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Catalaunian_Plains https://omniatlas.com/maps/europe/4510620/)

claim: In 452 CE Attila invaded Italy; Pope Leo I met him, and Attila withdrew.
fact_check_evidence: Attila invaded Italy in 452; Pope Leo I met him near Mantua and Attila then withdrew. Why he withdrew (Leo, disease, supply) is debated, but the claim does not assert a cause. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_I https://www.medievalists.net/2015/05/why-did-attila-leave-italy/)

claim: Attila died in 453 CE, and his empire of many peoples soon fell apart.
fact_check_evidence: Attila died in 453; his sons fought over the succession and after the Gepid-led revolt at Nedao (454) the Hunnic empire quickly collapsed. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attila https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nedao)

claim: Christian writers called Attila the “Scourge of God.”
pre_check: Confirm the page gives the epithet.
fact_check_evidence: Attila became known as the 'Scourge of God' (flagellum Dei) in Christian tradition, which saw his invasions as divine punishment. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attila https://www.livescience.com/44417-attila-the-hun.html)

claim: In 455 CE the Vandals sacked Rome for two weeks.
fact_check_evidence: Gaiseric's Vandals plundered Rome for fourteen days (2 to 16 June 455). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(455) https://omniatlas.com/maps/europe/4550602/)

claim: The word vandalism comes from the Vandals’ name.
fact_check_evidence: 'Vandalism' was coined as French vandalisme by Henri Gregoire in 1794, from the name of the Vandals. (https://www.etymonline.com/word/vandalism https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandalism)

claim: In 476 CE the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the young western emperor Romulus Augustulus.
fact_check_evidence: Odoacer, a Germanic commander of the barbarian troops in Italy, deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus on 4 September 476. (https://www.history.com/articles/last-roman-emperor-romulus-augustulus https://www.worldhistory.org/Odoacer/)

claim: Odoacer did not make himself emperor: he sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king.
fact_check_evidence: In 476 Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, sent the imperial regalia to Zeno in Constantinople and ruled Italy as king, nominally under the eastern emperor. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odoacer https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Odoacer)

claim: Romulus Augustulus bore the names of Rome’s founder and its first emperor; Augustulus means “little Augustus.”
fact_check_evidence: Romulus Augustus shared the names of Rome's founder and first emperor (likely coincidental); Augustulus is a diminutive meaning little Augustus. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus https://www.unrv.com/emperors/romulus-augustulus.php)

claim: Many historians see 476 CE as a convenient marker rather than a sudden end, since life in Italy went on much as before for many people.
fact_check_evidence: Sources describe 476 (deposition of Romulus Augustulus by Odoacer) as a convenient or symbolic date; decline unfolded over decades and ordinary Romans would not have noticed a change; Odoacer kept working with the Senate. (https://jnnielsen.medium.com/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire-530a556ae114 https://courses.lumenlearning.com/atd-herkimer-westerncivilization/chapter/odoacer-and-the-fall-of-rome/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historiography_of_the_fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire)

claim: Historians have proposed many different reasons for the fall of the Western Empire.
fact_check_evidence: Alexander Demandt catalogued 210 reasons proposed for the fall of the Western Roman Empire. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historiography_of_the_fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire https://www.thehistoryblog.com/archives/102)

claim: Pressure from Germanic peoples and the Huns stretched the western army beyond its limits.
fact_check_evidence: The Huns drove Germanic peoples across the frontiers and later attacked directly; the western army could not expel them and became few and ineffective. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire https://www.britannica.com/topic/barbarian-invasions)

claim: Repeated civil wars between Roman generals weakened the West from within.
fact_check_evidence: Historians note near-endemic civil war from the late 2nd to 5th centuries CE, which sapped the army and made the West more vulnerable to external threats. (https://blog.oup.com/2022/10/civil-war-and-the-end-of-the-roman-empire/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire)

claim: The Vandals’ capture of Carthage in 439 CE cost the West its richest tax base and a major grain supply.
fact_check_evidence: The Vandals took Carthage on 19 October 439; Africa was the West's wealthiest region (Heather's 'jugular vein') and a key grain source for Rome. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Carthage_(439) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandal_conquest_of_Roman_Africa)

claim: Edward Gibbon’s The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire blamed, in part, the rise of Christianity and a loss of civic virtue.
fact_check_evidence: Gibbon attributed decline partly to Christianity and a loss of civic virtue, alongside barbarian pressure and other causes; 'in part' is accurate. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_History_of_the_Decline_and_Fall_of_the_Roman_Empire https://www.washingtonindependentreviewofbooks.com/index.php/features/idecline-and-fall-of-the-roman-empire-i-by-edward-gibbon-an-appreciation)

claim: Some historians describe the period as a transformation into the kingdoms of medieval Europe rather than a sudden collapse.
fact_check_evidence: Peter Brown and the 'late antiquity' school frame the period as transformation rather than sudden collapse; 'some historians' reflects that this is one side of a debate. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_antiquity https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/189589.The_World_of_Late_Antiquity)

claim: The East was richer and more populous than the West, which helps explain why it survived.
fact_check_evidence: Sources note the East was more populous, more urbanized and produced more tax revenue (Egypt, trade routes), commonly cited among reasons it survived. (https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/History/World_History/Western_Civilization_1e_-_A_Concise_History_I_(Brooks)/13%3A_Byzantium/13.01%3A_East_Versus_West https://oyc.yale.edu/node/1395)

claim: Historians call the Eastern Roman Empire the Byzantine Empire, but its people called themselves Romans.
fact_check_evidence: 'Byzantine' is a later scholarly label (16th century); the empire's inhabitants called themselves Rhomaioi, Romans. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire https://www.medievalists.net/2026/04/byzantines-romans/)

claim: Over time Greek replaced Latin as the language of the eastern empire’s government.
fact_check_evidence: Greek gradually replaced Latin as the language of administration in the eastern empire, a shift largely complete by the Heraclian period (7th century). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire_under_the_Heraclian_dynasty https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Greek)

claim: In the 6th century CE, Justinian reconquered Italy and North Africa for a time.
fact_check_evidence: Justinian's generals retook North Africa from the Vandals (533 to 534) and Italy from the Ostrogoths (535 to 554), but Lombards took much of Italy from 568. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire_under_the_Justinian_dynasty https://www.thecollector.com/what-was-justinian-reconquest/)

claim: Justinian built the great church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, finished in 537 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Justinian had Hagia Sophia rebuilt after the Nika riots (532); the church was completed and inaugurated in December 537. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia https://smarthistory.org/hagia-sophia-istanbul/)

claim: Sultan Mehmed II led the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453 to Ottoman forces led by Sultan Mehmed II after a siege of about 55 days. (https://www.britannica.com/event/Fall-of-Constantinople-1453 https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mehmed-II-Ottoman-sultan)

claim: The United States Senate takes its name from the Roman Senate.
pre_check: Confirm the page notes the Roman origin of the name.
fact_check_evidence: The word senate derives from Latin senatus (council of elders), the Roman body; the US Senate's name follows this Roman precedent. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/word-histories-from-congress)

claim: The United States Capitol is named after Rome’s Capitoline Hill.
pre_check: Confirm the page gives the origin of the name.
fact_check_evidence: Jefferson chose the name 'Capitol', from Latin Capitolium, invoking the Temple of Jupiter on Rome's Capitoline Hill; the land had been called Jenkins Hill. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitoline_Hill)

claim: The word veto is still used for the power to block laws, as when a US president vetoes a bill.
fact_check_evidence: Veto is Latin for 'I forbid', from Roman tribunes' power; the US president's power to reject bills is commonly called a veto. (https://www.etymonline.com/word/veto https://www.history.com/articles/veto)

claim: The framers of the US Constitution studied the Roman Republic and its balance between different parts of government.
pre_check: Confirm the page discusses classical influence.
fact_check_evidence: Scholarship documents that the framers drew on Polybius's and Cicero's account of Rome's mixed constitution when designing checks and balances. (https://gould.usc.edu/why/students/orgs/ilj/assets/docs/17-3%20Bederman.pdf https://digitalcommons.coastal.edu/jops/vol38/iss1/2/)

claim: Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles.
fact_check_evidence: Roman towns and camps commonly used an orthogonal grid with the cardo and decumanus crossing at right angles near the forum. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decumanus https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_plan)

claim: Many European cities grew from Roman towns or forts, including London, Paris, Cologne and Vienna.
pre_check: Confirm or cite city pages.
fact_check_evidence: London (Londinium) and Cologne (Colonia) were Roman foundations, but Paris (Lutetia of the Parisii) and Vienna (Celtic Vindobona area) had pre-Roman Celtic settlements before Roman towns/forts grew there. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutetia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Vienna)

claim: Neoclassical architecture copied Roman columns, domes and temple fronts in buildings across Europe and the Americas.
fact_check_evidence: Neoclassical architecture revived Greek and Roman columns, temple-front porticoes and domes, e.g. the Pantheon in Paris and the US Capitol. (https://www.archivinci.com/blogs/what-is-neoclassical-architecture https://architectureofcities.com/neoclassical-architecture)

claim: Latin mottoes still appear on seals and coins, such as “E pluribus unum,” “out of many, one,” on the Great Seal of the United States.
fact_check_evidence: E pluribus unum, meaning out of many, one, appears on the Great Seal adopted in 1782 and is printed on most US coinage. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/E-pluribus-unum-United-States-motto https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Seal_of_the_United_States)

claim: Much of Roman history comes from ancient writers such as Livy, Tacitus and Suetonius, who had their own sources, purposes and biases.
fact_check_evidence: Scholars note Livy's moralizing aims, Tacitus's hostility to Domitian and Suetonius's senatorial bias and uneven sources. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twelve_Caesars https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacitean_studies)

claim: Huge numbers of Latin inscriptions carved in stone record laws, careers, dedications and epitaphs.
fact_check_evidence: The Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum holds about 180,000 inscriptions, including religious dedications, imperial and honorific texts and epitaphs, illuminating all aspects of Roman life. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Inscriptionum_Latinarum https://cil.bbaw.de/en/homenavigation/the-cil/inscriptions-in-the-roman-world)

claim: Coins help historians date events and show how emperors wanted to be seen.
fact_check_evidence: Coins bearing emperors' names and titles are key tools for dating, and imperial coinage broadcast the emperor's chosen image and messages. (https://sites.rhodes.edu/coins/study-roman-coins https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/article/propaganda-on-roman-coins/)

claim: Archaeology reveals ordinary lives that writers ignored, from houses and graves to rubbish heaps.
fact_check_evidence: Excavations of houses, cesspits and rubbish deposits, and burials have yielded evidence on ordinary Romans' diet and lives that the literary record largely omits. (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/110623-ancient-rome-human-waste-herculaneum-science-diet-excrement-italy https://phys.org/news/2012-01-ancient-pompeii-trash-tombs.html)

claim: Roman history spans more than 2,000 years, from the traditional founding in 753 BCE to the fall of Constantinople in 1453 CE.
fact_check_evidence: Sources describe over 2,000 years of Roman history from the traditional 753 BC founding to the fall of Constantinople (Eastern Roman Empire) in 1453. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Roman_Empire https://www.history.com/topics/ancient-rome/ancient-rome)

claim: A recurring pattern in Roman history is that whoever controlled the army controlled the state.
fact_check_evidence: Historians note that from the late Republic on, legions' loyalty to generals and later emperors made army support the real foundation of political power. (https://wou.edu/history/files/2015/08/andrewwhite.pdf https://www.unrv.com/articles/roman-republic-vs-roman-empire-what-changed.php)
